", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes"], "ref": "s48", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "3f1ab036-5423-418c-82f3-db208d02cb8a", "content": "## 6. Breach and incident references

This section sets how Wickhold may talk about breaches and other public incidents, in any channel.

1. Never name a victim. That covers company names, product names, and descriptions that identify one ("a large regional retailer in the week it made the news").
2. No humor. Not in the copy, not in the image, not in a speaker's aside.
3. Nothing within 30 days of a public incident. Count from the first public disclosure. For the 30 days, Wickhold does not publish, post, send or sponsor anything that refers to the incident or that is plainly timed to it. An incident is not a marketing hook.

After 30 days, a breach may be discussed in general terms only, as a pattern and without identifying anyone. A technical analysis of a technique is fine if it does not rely on the incident for attention.

The rules cover paid media, social, email, blog posts, sales sequences, talks and replies to journalists. They apply to personal LinkedIn accounts when the post mentions Wickhold or its products. Press inquiries about a live incident go to Ilse Varga-Holm, and nobody comments before she has spoken to me.

If a campaign in market could be read as a reaction to a new public incident, whoever notices it pauses it and tells Ilse. Nobody will be criticized for pausing. Sales may answer a direct customer question about an incident with facts about the customer's own deployment. It may not use the question as an opening.

Incidents at Wickhold customers are never discussed without the customer's written approval, whatever their age. The approved Lowmoor material is the model. It has a figure and no drama.

Not approved:

> After last week's breach at a regional bank, can your team afford another six hours?

Approved, more than 30 days after any related event:

> When a pod misbehaves, Wickhold Quenchline in contain mode can isolate its network while the on-call engineer works out what happened.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "6. Breach and incident references"], "ref": "s49", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "400b4601-2eb7-4751-91d5-62bce3820026", "content": "## 2. Mission

**Keep small failures from becoming big ones.**

The mission is written for the people who run production. A failed deployment, a process that should not be running, a credential in the wrong place: these happen every week in any serious cluster, and they stay dull when somebody contains them early. The company exists to keep them dull.

Three things follow from that wording, and they are the reasons it was chosen.

It accepts that failures happen. A company that claims failures will not happen has stopped talking to engineers. Founders Maren and Dov spent years as on-call infrastructure leads before starting Wickhold in Denver in March 2019, and neither of them has ever met a system that did not fail.

It measures success by size. A contained incident still gets logged, reviewed and fixed. The win is that it stayed at one pod and did not reach the node, or stayed at one node and did not reach the cluster.

It says "keep", which is ongoing work. Containment is something a team does with good tools, every week. The mission gives the product a role in that work and leaves the credit for the outcome with the customer's on-call team.

Use the mission on recruiting pages, in all-hands decks and in the opening of long-form pieces about the company. It is an internal compass first. It should not be pasted on product pages as a slogan, because the tagline already does that job.

A few sentences show the difference between using the mission and hanging it on the wall.

Good, from a recruiting page: "We build software that keeps small failures from becoming big ones. If you have been paged at 3am, you already know why that matters."

Weak: "Our mission is to revolutionize the way the world thinks about failure." It's bigger than the company, and it says nothing an on-call engineer would recognize.

Sales, this is the sheet to use before you answer a security questionnaire. If a deck or an old email says something different, the deck or the email is out of date.

| Program | Status | What you may say |
|---|---|---|
| SOC 2 Type II | Held. Renewed January 2026 | "Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II." |
| FedRAMP Moderate | In process. Not held | "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." |

**FedRAMP.** Never claim FedRAMP authorization or certification. The approved wording above is the only wording. It goes in copy exactly as written, including the word "pursuing".

These are banned in every channel, spoken or written: "FedRAMP Authorized", "FedRAMP certified", "FedRAMP Ready", "FedRAMP compliant", "FedRAMP equivalent", "built to FedRAMP standards". Agency buyers read those words literally, and a false statement to a federal buyer is a contract and legal problem, whatever the deal size.

The status changes when authorization is complete and published, and this sheet says so. An assessor's visit, a sponsor conversation, or a positive meeting does not change it. Do not give prospects a target date. We do not publish one. If a federal prospect presses, the answer is the sentence above and an offer to connect them with me.

Good, in an answer to a questionnaire:

> Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026. Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization. We can share the SOC 2 report under NDA.

Bad:

> We're basically FedRAMP Authorized, the paperwork is just finishing up.

**SOC 2.** The report goes out under NDA through the account team, never by public link. Say "Type II" every time. Say "held" or "renewed", and do not say "SOC 2 certified", because SOC 2 ends in an attestation report and not a certificate.

**Questionnaires and RFPs.** Security questionnaires go through the account team, and any answer about certifications is copied from this sheet. If a form offers only "Yes" or "No" for FedRAMP, answer "No", and use the comments box for the approved sentence. Do not tick a box in the hope of explaining later.

**A blog post on draining nodes before an upgrade.** The writer finds a warm photo of a rack door. The title and tags look right and `restrictions` is empty. At full size, the photo is clean and it passes. It needs a crop, so the writer checks `width` and `height` first and confirms the focal point stays in frame.

**A dark section on a pricing comparison page.** The designer drops in a spot illustration that looked good on the last page. The record says `background: transparent` and `safe_on: light`, so it fails on this band. The record has no `variant_of`, but another record points at it as a parent, and that sibling is `safe_on: dark`. Problem solved in two minutes.

**A customer webinar invitation.** The perfect team photo has a line in `restrictions` that the writer almost skipped, because the thumbnail looked fine and the image had been used on the website last year. The line changes the answer. The image stays out, whatever last year's page did, and the writer picks again.

Accessible work is part of the brand standard, and it is checked at review alongside everything else. The reasoning is simple enough: engineers read documentation on bad monitors, on phones and at 3am, and some of them have low vision or are color-blind. Work that only functions in perfect conditions fails the people it is meant for.

In summary, four commitments apply across all marketing work:

- Text is readable against its background. The palette has been measured, and not every pairing is suitable for small text. Ember in particular needs care.
- Images carry a text description, so nobody loses the point of a piece because an image did not load or cannot be seen.
- Meaning is never carried by color alone. A chart or status needs a label, a shape or a pattern too.
- Pages work with a keyboard and at high zoom, and video has captions.

The misses that come up most at review are predictable. A chart legend that relies on Ember versus Verdigris alone is hard to read for some color-blind readers, since those two are close in lightness. An Ember link in a paragraph looks fine on a designer's monitor and is hard to read on a laptop in daylight. Text set into an image can't be read by a screen reader and can't be translated. Video exported from a webinar tool often ships with captions switched off.

Accessibility review belongs to whoever does the brand check on a piece, and it isn't a separate stage. If a template fails, Noor's team fixes the template, so the same miss doesn't come back in every piece made from it.

The specific requirements are in the visual accessibility guidance, and the measured color pairs are in the logo and color addendum. Bricolage Grotesque's limit on small sizes, in section 8, is as much an accessibility point as a matter of taste.

1. **The fact.** What shipped, what was measured, what happened. Put the number here if there is one.
2. **The context.** Two or three sentences on why it matters to someone running clusters or answering for them.
3. **The way out.** One link, with a short instruction in front of it.

Then stop. If you have a second point, it is a second post next week.

Tallow replaced White as the ground. It is warmer, it photographs well beside the current imagery, and it keeps a page from feeling like a blank dashboard. The mark is a geometric W whose center stroke rises as a wick, tipped by one Ember dot. It says the same thing as the brand idea: a straight, deliberate structure with one small, controlled point of heat at the top. The dot is the only warm thing in the mark, and that is the reason to protect it. Used alongside the wordmark "Wickhold", it forms the lockup, which is the default in most layouts.

There are four approved variants: ink on transparent, reversed on transparent, on a Tallow panel, and on a Soot panel. Exact file specifications, clear space and minimum sizes are in the logo and color addendum. How to choose among the variants for a given layout belongs to the logo-in-context guidance.

The 2024 shield-and-flame logo is retired. It still appears in the archive and in a few old files, and it should not be used in anything new.

The logo appears once in a layout, and it usually doesn't need to be large. Confidence in a mark shows in how much room it's given, so a modest logo with space around it is better than a big one crowded by other elements. In the product, the mark appears in the console header and on the sign-in page. Screens that a customer works in all day don't need it anywhere else.

Two pieces of history are worth keeping in mind. In the first month after launch, the product team shipped a loading state with a flickering dot, and customers read it as an error. It was withdrawn. The dot does not move. And early on, several people tried turning the W into a pattern for backgrounds and swag. The mark loses its meaning when it repeats, because the whole point is that there is one of it. Use it once per layout.

The company did not change what it builds. Quenchline has offered detection and containment since September 2020. What changed is which half of that sentence the brand leads with. In the 2024 identity, the watching came first and containment was a feature. In the 2026 identity, containment is the point and detection is what makes it possible. Detection still matters to buyers and should be described accurately. It just isn't the headline.

Evenburn fits the same logic from the other direction. Posture work reduces how much there is to catch fire, and it gives the team a fix order so that the worst exposure path gets closed first. The story to tell is about keeping the fuel down, and it shouldn't be told as a second, separate product category.

Leashgate extends the idea to AI agents, which now take actions inside customers' environments. An agent with broad tools is a new kind of workload that can make a mistake quickly. Leashgate sets out what that agent may do and keeps a record of what it did. It is in early access, and the position should be described with that in mind: a direction the company is working in, with real customers trying it.

Slide titles use Bricolage Grotesque at 40 pt or larger, and body text in Plex Sans never goes below 18 pt. The master deck template and the document templates have all of this built in, so start there. Fonts should come from the shared font folder, because a copy downloaded from elsewhere can be a different version and shift the line breaks in someone else's slides.

A piece of long-form writing, such as a report, can use Plex Sans for captions and pull quotes. Pull quotes stay in Plex Sans and are not an excuse for a third display style.

- **Wickhold Containment Report.** Annual, published in April. It was the Wickhold Field Report before 2025. Reports use the company's visual identity with no separate report logo.
- **Slow Burn Summit.** Wickhold's own customer conference, in Denver each September. The 2026 edition ran September 15 to 16. The event may have its own title treatment, set in the brand type, and it uses the Wickhold logo.

Webinars, workshops and one-off programs are described in plain words and do not get a brand of their own. A proposal for a podcast with its own name and cover art was turned down last year for this reason. A topic that needs its own identity to be interesting probably isn't interesting.

One of the company values, and the one marketing finds hardest. Every product we sell has an edge. Wickhold Evenburn finds drift and exposure paths; it does not contain anything. Quenchline contains what is running; it does not patch the image it came from. Saying so costs a little in the moment and buys a lot of belief for the next claim on the page. Engineers look for the catch. When they find we already named it, they keep reading.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Admit limits"], "ref": "s70", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "5bce8648-d3e6-4352-a0ff-0023d9af46b9", "content": "## Contrast: 4.5:1 for text

Text on any image or graphic meets at least 4.5:1 against what is directly behind it. We apply the same floor to all sizes, including large headlines. A designer will point out that the web standard relaxes for large type. We know. The single number is easier to check, and a stat card shrinks to thumbnail size in a feed, where large type stops being large. This floor governs images. Layouts follow the logo and color addendum.

Measured ratios for the palette:

| Pair | Ratio | Text allowed? |
|---|---|---|
| Soot on Tallow | 15.5:1 | Yes |
| Tallow on Soot | 15.5:1 | Yes |
| Whetstone on Tallow | 4.8:1 | Yes |
| Verdigris on Soot | 4.5:1 | Yes, just. Test your export |
| Ember on Tallow | 4.1:1 | No |
| Soot on Ember | 3.8:1 | No |
| Ember on Soot | 3.8:1 | No |
| Tallow on Ember | 4.1:1 | No |
| Verdigris on Tallow | 3.4:1 | No |
| Whetstone on Soot | 3.2:1 | No |

This surprises people: Ember does not carry text on our grounds, and no text sits on Ember in an image. Ember is for shapes, rules and the focal element. Headlines on Tallow are Soot. Headlines on Soot are Tallow.

Over a photo, measure against the lightest spot behind the letters for Tallow text and the darkest spot for Soot text. An even-looking dark photo often has one bright lamp right under the word. If the text fails anywhere, put it on a solid Soot or Tallow panel. Do not add a gradient scrim: our illustration and graphic language has no gradients, and scrims tend to fail at their edges anyway.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline can isolate a pod's network the moment a known-bad process starts. Your team sets which actions run on their own."

Good: "Small fires stay small."

Bad: "Total protection for everything you run." This promises what no product can deliver, and it could be anyone's line.

Bad: "Attackers are already inside your cluster. Are you ready?" This is fear, and the question does nothing for the reader.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "1. What changed in 2026", "How the change rolled out"], "ref": "s74", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "5e4d5b12-2225-41f6-b56a-3715f0299066", "content": "## When the news is ours

We will have our own bad days: a bad agent release, a late fix, a false containment that drained a node it should have left alone. The values cover this before anything else does. Say what happened. Contain first. Admit limits. Leave it better for the next on-call.

In practice:

- Lead with what happened to the customer's systems, in their terms.
- Use "we" and an active verb. "We shipped a policy update that drained nodes it should not have." "An issue occurred" is not a sentence we publish.
- Apologize once, plainly, in one short sentence. Then get on with the facts.
- Say what is still unknown.
- Say when the next update comes, and hit that time even if there's nothing new.

Dov signs off anything technical. Priit Salonen reads anything that touches a contract. Nobody in marketing edits the facts for tone.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "When the news is ours"], "ref": "s75", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "5e56a337-029a-4106-88ee-ccfbe4044d6d", "content": "### Photography

Photographs show real work in real places: available light, working rooms and real infrastructure, warm and slightly underexposed. The feeling to aim for is the quiet of a team that has things under control, late in the day, with the lights half on. People are shown doing what they actually do. The 2024 look of bright, staged collaboration has gone, as has its blue tint.

A useful test is to ask whether an on-call engineer would recognize the room. A cable tray with a handwritten label passes. A spotless corridor of lights does not.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Photography"], "ref": "s76", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "63250d81-fd52-48b4-90ff-f2aea5b27906", "content": "## Banned terms

There are thirteen. They stay out of headlines, body copy, decks, alt text and speaker notes that leave the building. When one shows up in a draft it usually marks the spot where the writer ran out of facts, so deleting it rarely fixes the sentence. Find the fact.

| Term | Why it is out | What to do instead |
|---|---|---|
| seamless | Putting an eBPF agent on every node has seams: a kernel check, a Helm upgrade, a stretch in observe mode. Platform engineers know this and stop reading when told otherwise. | Say what the rollout takes. |
| robust | Strong against what? The word claims a result and skips the test. | Name the failure the thing survived. |
| leverage | A finance word doing a job that "use" does for free. | Use "use". |
| best-in-class | No class, no judge, no source. It cannot pass "say the number, then stop". | Give the figure and where it came from. |
| next-gen | Every product in this market has been next-gen at some point. The word ages the day it ships. | Say what it does on a node today. |
| single pane of glass | Our readers have been sold this pane many times and own several. It also describes watching, and the job here is containing. | Name the screen and what it shows. |
| holistic | Usually covering for a gap. If something spans cloud and cluster, those two words are shorter and checkable. | List what is covered. |
| unlock | Implies the customer's own work was locked up and we hold the key. Drags padlocks into the room as well. | Say what the reader can now do. |
| empower | The readers already have root. Nobody here hands out power. | Say what changed for them, in a verb they would use. |
| cutting-edge | A claim about us, and an undated one. eBPF is well past being new, and that is one reason it is safe to run in production. | Name the technique. |
| game-changing | An incident is nobody's game, and the claim has no number attached. | Give the before and after. |
| prevent all | A promise no security product can keep. Includes "prevents all", which is the same promise with better grammar. | See the verbs below. |
| stop all | Same promise, same problem. A CISO who reads this line once will discount the rest of the page. | See the verbs below. |

The prose test: if a sentence still reads as true after you swap the product for a toaster, it needed a fact and got an adjective.

", "heading_path": ["Word list", "Banned terms"], "ref": "s77", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md"}, {"chunk_id": "641a5f31-2bfc-40c7-abe3-a03717d897c4", "content": "## 3. Values

There are four, and they are written the way an on-call lead would say them.

**Say what happened.**
Report the event in plain order: what occurred, what was affected, what was done, what is next. This applies to incident reports, release notes, customer emails and the company's own mistakes. When a release goes badly, the customer note says so in the first sentence.

Good: "The last Wickhold Quenchline release raised CPU use on nodes running older kernels. A fix shipped on Tuesday. Here is how to check whether you were affected."

Bad: "We're always working to improve performance, and our latest update includes important enhancements."

**Contain first.**
In an incident, limit the damage before explaining it. In marketing, the same ordering applies: the first thing a reader gets is the thing that helps them, and the story of how it came about can wait. The value also sets the company's posture. Wickhold talks about containing, limiting and slowing. A promise of a world with no incidents is a promise no honest vendor can keep.

Good: "At Lowmoor Credit Union, time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

That example gives the result with no adjectives around it and leaves the reader to decide what it means.

**Admit limits.**
Every product has edges, and engineers find them within a week. Naming a limit in advance costs less than having a customer discover it during a bad night, and it makes everything else the company says easier to believe.

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline works at runtime. It does not review code before it ships."

**Leave it better for the next on-call.**
This one comes straight from the founders. When an on-call shift ends, the next person should find the runbook updated, the noisy alert tuned and the handoff note written. Inside marketing it means naming source files sensibly, recording why a decision was made, and putting a correction in the document that was wrong and not only in a thread. It is why the "tried and dropped" list in section 1 exists.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "3. Values"], "ref": "s78", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "64d6d696-ec4f-4e0f-bd79-0d600e9cfca7", "content": "## Preferred terms

**Workload, not asset.** Customers run workloads, and that is the word they use in their own runbooks. "Asset" comes from inventory spreadsheets and suggests a thing that sits still. A workload moves, restarts and misbehaves, which is why it needs a runtime product. Inside the marketing team "asset" still means a blog post or an image file; that use never reaches a customer.

**Contain, limit and slow, rather than prevent.** This is the company's argument in three verbs. Something will go wrong on a Tuesday night regardless of what anyone buys. Wickhold Quenchline contains what is already running. Wickhold Evenburn limits exposure. Wickhold Leashgate limits what an agent can reach. "Slow" is the honest verb when the action buys time and does not end the problem. Also keep "eliminate" and "eradicate" out of it; they are "prevent" in a bigger coat.

Use "contain" only when a containment action actually happens. Detection on its own is detection.

One exception came out of a release-notes review. A line saying a patch prevents a crash in the agent is describing our own bug, so it can stay. The rule covers promises about what happens to customers, and a changelog entry makes none.

**Customers, not clients.** Clients have an account manager and a lunch. Customers run our agent in production and page us. A "client" in the software sense stays: `kubectl` is a client, an email client is a client. "Users" is fine when you mean the people logged in to the console, because a customer is the whole company.

", "heading_path": ["Word list", "Preferred terms"], "ref": "s79", "relative_path": "brand/voice/word-list.md"}, {"chunk_id": "664b063b-3dba-4a39-be64-6af03fbfbb25", "content": "### Order of authority

When two sources conflict, the higher one on this list wins:

1. **Legal-approved claims.** The approved claims, certification status, regional rules and customer quote policy owned by Priit Salonen, General Counsel.
2. **These 2026 guidelines**, together with the logo and color addendum, which has the same standing.
3. **Channel playbooks.** The working guides for each channel.
4. **Everything else.** This includes the voice and style documents, messaging, personas, product overviews, templates, sales material, meeting notes and Slack.

So the order is: legal-approved claims, then the 2026 guidelines, then channel playbooks, then everything else.

A lower source is not void. It applies wherever nothing above it speaks to the question. A template's rule, or a decision recorded in meeting notes or Slack by the person who owns the topic, is followed like any other rule until a higher source contradicts it. The order settles conflicts and does not rank importance. If a document at the bottom of the list has the only rule on a subject, that is the rule.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Order of authority"], "ref": "s80", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "668f858f-133e-4581-b3b0-c0ca0a2f6f13", "content": "## Founder voice and brand voice

There are two voices at Wickhold, and they have one hard line between them.

**Founder voice is first person singular, and it is signed.** Maren writes as "I". Her posts carry her name. She gets to have feelings and doubts, tell a story from a bad night in 2017, and be wrong in public. Dov's technical posts work the same way and are signed "Dov".

**Brand voice never says "I" or "we think".** Website, product pages, company LinkedIn, the company X account, email, decks, reports: no first person singular, ever. "We believe", "we feel" and "in our view" are "we think" in different shoes, and they go too.

**Brand voice uses "Wickhold" or "we" for facts only.** Things that happened, things that are true of the company, things a lawyer could check.

| Fine in brand voice | Not in brand voice |
|---|---|
| We renewed SOC 2 Type II in January 2026. | We think SOC 2 matters. |
| Wickhold serves more than 140 customers. | I've talked to a lot of platform teams. |
| Containment is where incidents are won or lost. | We believe containment is where incidents are won or lost. |

The third row is the useful one. Brand voice still holds opinions. It states them as flat sentences, the way the on-call lead does, and lets the reader disagree. "We think" adds nothing except a hedge.

Practicalities. Nobody else writes as "I" in Wickhold content. Kofi's developer posts and anything from the wider team run in brand voice under a byline, because a byline is credit and a founder post is a person speaking for themselves. Customer quotes are quotes and say whatever was approved. If the content team drafts for Maren, she reads it and changes it before her name goes on, and a post that she has not read does not go out. In the spring a joint Maren-and-Dov byline was tried on one post; "I" became unreadable after two paragraphs, so that was dropped. One author per post.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Founder voice and brand voice"], "ref": "s81", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "6b2f30da-423b-4eae-8725-3f1eae6d3b11", "content": "## Choosing by post type

| Post | Hero |
|---|---|
| Founder essay, signed by Maren | Photo of a working room, or a quiet illustration |
| Technical post by Dov or the engineering team | Infrastructure photo or a concept illustration tied to the mechanism |
| Customer story | Photo from that customer's site if released, otherwise an illustration. Never a stand-in photo that implies it is their site |
| Containment Report findings | Illustration. Save the charts for the body |
| Comparison post | Neutral illustration. No competitor logos or product screens |
| Incident analysis or a post about a breach | Quiet illustration without flame, or an empty-room photo. Keep it plain |

The hero is chosen for the idea in the post. A post on default containment policies should not get a generic "engineer with laptop". Find the one object that matches: a tray under a wick, a closed rack door, a hand on a breaker.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "Changes"], "ref": "s83", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "71def5fd-8e65-4813-946c-8576df1c15d3", "content": "## 2. First lines

**No rhetorical question as the first line of any asset.** Blog post, landing page hero, email (subject line and first sentence both), LinkedIn post, X post, video script, slide one of a deck.

"Is your cluster ready for the next incident?" tells the reader nothing and asks them to do the writer's work. It's also the most common opening in our category, so it reads as noise. Open on a fact, an event or a claim.

| Don't open with | Open with |
|---|---|
| What would you do if a pod started a shell at 3am? | A pod in `checkout` started a shell at 03:14 UTC. |
| Tired of alert fatigue? | Most alerts at 3am are about something that already stopped mattering. |

Real questions later in a piece are fine. An FAQ section is full of them and that's what it is for, as long as the page opens on a statement.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "2. First lines"], "ref": "s84", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "735363d2-23db-4b36-862e-fc0dfa852067", "content": "### Testing a campaign idea

Before a concept goes to design, Ilse's team asks four questions of it.

1. Could any other security vendor run this with their logo on it? If so, it isn't the position.
2. Does it depend on the reader being scared? If so, drop it.
3. Does it show containment, or only talk about it?
4. Would the customer's on-call lead forward it to a colleague without a sarcastic comment?

The "Quiet night" concept from the 2026 launch passed all four, and it became the opening of the launch film: a dark office, one screen, a log line reading that a pod had been isolated, and an engineer who doesn't appear because she is asleep at home.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Testing a campaign idea"], "ref": "s85", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "758a650b-e384-4440-b0e9-7ecda7e6ee6c", "content": "### Where the category goes wrong

Security marketing has habits that readers have learned to skip. The position is partly defined by not having them.

| Category habit | What Wickhold does |
|---|---|
| Opens with a frightening scenario | Opens with what a team can do about the problem |
| Promises total coverage | Says what is covered and names what is not |
| Sells the dashboard | Shows the containment action and its log entry |
| Treats the on-call engineer as a victim | Treats the on-call engineer as the expert |
| Uses a survey to alarm | Uses a survey to size a problem, then stops |

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Where the category goes wrong"], "ref": "s86", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "759e0fbd-e00d-4a0b-887f-7d61d89145c3", "content": "### What replaced Cobalt

Cobalt, the primary color from 2024, was retired on February 10, 2026, and **Ember `#C2501F` replaced it as the primary color**. Cobalt should not appear in any new work. Ember is not used the way Cobalt was. Cobalt covered whole slides, hero bands and booth walls. Ember is a small, deliberate point of heat, and a layout built around it should look mostly like Tallow or Soot.

The reasons for the change were practical as well as symbolic. The category is full of blue, and in side-by-side tests of competitor pages Wickhold's old pages were hard to pick out. A warm orange-brown also ties the color to the brand idea, since it is the color of a banked coal. It is deliberately neither a bright hazard orange nor an alarm red, because the brand is not trying to raise a reader's pulse.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "What replaced Cobalt"], "ref": "s87", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "76bbbcb1-53e8-43a0-a87a-749d22eecce8", "content": "## 16. Headlines that get sent back

A short list from the last year of review comments, so you can save yourself the round trip.

- "The ultimate guide to" anything. It won't be.
- "X things every platform engineer should know". They know.
- "Why containment matters". Say what it changes.
- "Introducing". The reader can see that it's new. Say what it does.
- Any headline that would also fit a competitor's blog. Swap their name into your mental picture and check.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "16. Headlines that get sent back"], "ref": "s88", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "76df2e0e-6e05-4285-bede-8b07fece0fb3", "content": "## Picking an image: the order

1. Decide the category and read that page.
2. Decide the content type and read that page.
3. Search the library. Search by description and by a few different words, since tags are uneven.
4. Open the record. Read `restrictions` and `usage_rights` first, then `background`, `safe_on` and size.
5. Look at the picture itself at full size against the current identity. Metadata does not catch everything.
6. Check it against the rest of the layout, on the real ground.
7. Add it to the draft with its `id` noted in the review comment, so Brand can trace it.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Picking an image: the order"], "ref": "s89", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "77fbbc82-d712-4859-a1c7-32f1301168fd", "content": "**The Containment Report.** Annual, every April, and the most formal thing we publish. It reads like a clinical note: findings in flat declaratives, method stated early, no pitch in the body. The product can appear at the end, briefly, once the reader has had what they came for.

**Release notes.** Past tense, specific, no selling. A bug we fixed is described as a bug.

**Press.** Third person, plain, one idea per release. The quote from Maren is the only place with any warmth, and she writes it herself.

**Sales decks and talk tracks.** Same facts, same claims, slightly warmer because a person is in the room. If a slide would embarrass the on-call lead, it comes out.

**Webinars and video.** Script it as speech, then cut a third. Two people talking through a real incident timeline beats one person reading slides. No stock intro music with a heartbeat in it, and no voiceover that sounds like a trailer.

**Support replies.** These are written by the support team and we don't police them, but the same habit applies: repeat what you saw, say what you did, say what happens next. A reply that begins by thanking the customer for their patience has already lost them.

**Events.** Slow Burn Summit in Denver is the one place where we are among friends, and it can sound like that. The stage voice is relaxed and first-name, and the facts on the slides are still the facts. Field Day is smaller and closer to a conversation in a car park. Booth copy is brand voice: short, mechanical, no shouting.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "ref": "s90", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "785f8389-2bfc-49d0-8c8c-858c1dfe7379", "content": "## Credit and caption

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning"], "ref": "s94", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7ebb4833-c358-4e50-aa82-4fa58d196656", "content": "# Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)

Pinned for the web team after three separate spellings turned up on one page.

Full form on first mention, short form after. First mention means the first place the name appears in a piece, and a headline counts.

| First mention | After that |
|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Quenchline |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Evenburn |
| Wickhold Leashgate | Leashgate |

One capital each. Never QuenchLine, EvenBurn or LeashGate. No internal caps, no hyphens, no all-caps in slides or nav.

Each piece starts over. A blog post that says Wickhold Quenchline does not earn the short form in the email promoting it.

Evenburn took its name on March 2, 2026. Don't write the former name in current copy, including "formerly" lines. Support handles customers who still ask for it.

Right: "Wickhold Evenburn ranks drift by exposure path. Evenburn does not contain anything at runtime."

Wrong: "Evenburn ranks drift" as the opening line, with the full name saved for the footer.

Nav labels and pricing table rows can use the short form. The page's first heading or sentence still uses the full one.

Never combine products into one name ("Quenchline-Evenburn suite"). There is no suite. If you mean more than one, name them.

**Company:** Wickhold. "Wickhold Security" retired with the rebrand on February 10, 2026. Wickhold, Inc. appears in contracts and legal footers and nowhere else.

**Lowercase, always:** contain mode, observe mode, containment action, default containment policy, drift, exposure path, fix order, tool-call policy, agent identity. These are concepts, not features with a logo.

**Capitalized:** tiers (Core, Team, Enterprise), Slow Burn Summit, Field Day, Wickhold Containment Report. "The report" on second reference, lowercase. Series A and Series B take capitals; SOC 2 Type II is set as shown.

Possessives are fine (Quenchline's agent). Skip the article: "Quenchline contains", never "the Quenchline".

The report had a different name before 2025: Wickhold Field Report. Keep that name when citing an edition that carried it. Don't rename old editions.

Feature names don't get "Wickhold" in front of them, and they don't get a trademark symbol. Neither do the products in running copy.

Lowercase product names only in code, where the tool demands it.

A draft that came through in May, lightly disguised:

> We're excited to announce that we think our powerful new drift capabilities will transform how modern teams approach cloud risk, giving you the confidence you need in an increasingly dangerous world.

The edit went like this.

"We're excited to announce" went first. The reader's interest in our excitement is zero.

"We think" is out, because this is brand voice.

"Powerful", "new" and "modern" were doing nothing. Remove them and the sentence gets more honest and no less informative.

"Increasingly dangerous world" is the fear habit, and it also isn't something we can source.

That left "drift capabilities will transform how teams approach cloud risk", which on inspection means nothing. So the reviewer asked the only useful question: what does a person see on the screen? The product manager's answer became the copy.

> Wickhold Evenburn lists the drift in a cluster and ranks it by exposure path, so the fix order is on one page. It does not contain anything at runtime.

That is shorter, it can be checked, and it names an edge. Nobody involved felt that it was a loss.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography"], "ref": "s97", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "80b784b5-ed7e-43ee-b94b-c4b9f387f3b3", "content": "### GDPR wording

Never say "GDPR compliant". Not about Wickhold, its products, its customers' deployments or any feature. The ban began with EU and UK copy and it now applies everywhere, including US pages that a European buyer can obviously read.

The approved wording is:

> Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations.

Use it as written. GDPR obligations belong to the controller and the processor and depend on what they do with the data. No vendor product can make a customer compliant, and a regulator or a procurement lawyer will read the phrase as a promise.

Variants that have turned up in drafts, all refused:

- "GDPR-ready"
- "fully GDPR aligned"
- "compliant with EU privacy law"
- "UK GDPR certified"

If a UK reader needs the point spelled out, the approved sentence covers UK GDPR. Do not add a second claim.

Examples:

| Bad | Good |
|---|---|
| Our GDPR compliant platform keeps EU workloads safe. | Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |
| Quenchline makes your clusters GDPR compliant. | Wickhold Quenchline records each containment action with a timestamp. Wickhold supports customers' GDPR obligations. |

A word on tone. European security buyers we've met through Field Day meetups tend to ask for the document and not the promise, so a short, flat statement does better than a paragraph about how seriously we take privacy. If a page has one line on GDPR, the approved sentence is that line. Don't surround it with "privacy-first" or "by design", which raise the same problem in softer words.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "GDPR wording"], "ref": "s98", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "819d53ad-e32a-41b3-94ae-7ccd3f1cc7d5", "content": "### Everything else

- **Measurements take digits, always.** Anything with a unit: 220 nodes, 11 minutes, 7.4 hours, 90 days, 38 seconds, 1,900 nodes.
- **Counts of ordinary things** spell out one to nine and use digits from 10: "three clusters", "12 namespaces". Mixed in one sentence, go with digits.
- **Commas from 1,000 up.** No "1.9k nodes", not even on social.
- **Keep the decimal the source gave you.** 7.4 hours stays 7.4 hours. Don't round to "about seven hours", and don't add precision the source lacks.
- **Approved sentences stay as approved.** The report line says "more than six hours", spelled out, and that's how it runs in every piece. The same goes for "more than 140 customers", which never becomes "140+". Legal approved the sentence, and this guide doesn't get to tidy it.
- **Don't do arithmetic on claims.** Lowmoor went from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Do not convert that into a percentage or an "x times faster". The figures we can stand behind are the two figures we were given. Same for adding results from different customers together.
- **No "up to".** "Up to" numbers are a best case wearing a fact's clothes. Give the median, or say which run you mean.
- **No tildes or "approx."** in published copy. If a figure is an estimate, say "about".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Everything else"], "ref": "s99", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "849c4a03-5ccb-4481-baf9-1a0a8bee9d61", "content": "## The two rules that come up every week

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week"], "ref": "s100", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "85f52c31-27b5-4fe5-921a-ea411fb55932", "content": "## The image library and its metadata

Every approved image lives in the image library, and every image in it has a metadata record. Do not pick from the thumbnail grid and stop there. The thumbnail does not show you the limits on the image.

| Field | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `id`, `filename` | Identity. Filenames were set by different people across several years and tell you little. |
| `type`, `title` | Rough category and a human label. |
| `description` | What is in the picture. Often thin, sometimes empty. |
| `tags` | Search help. Inconsistent, so never treat a missing tag as meaning anything. |
| `usage_rights` | The grant we hold for the file. |
| `restrictions` | The limits on this particular image. See below. |
| `added_date` | When it entered the library, which is not when it was made. |
| `source`, `attribution` | Where it came from. In-house work reads `internal-production`, and `attribution` is usually empty or names the in-house team. Empty attribution means no credit line is needed. |
| `width`, `height` | Pixel size. Check before you plan a crop. |
| `background` | How the image relates to what sits behind it. See below. |
| `safe_on` | Which grounds it can sit on. See below. |
| `variant_of` | Points at the parent when the image is one version of another. |

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The image library and its metadata"], "ref": "s101", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "86969aea-4633-4607-bc0c-60994231516b", "content": "## 11. Governance

The folder contains documents from seven years, written by different people for different deadlines, and sometimes two of them disagree. |---|---|---|

Three layers, read in this order.

1. **This page.** Applies to everything.
2. **The category.** What kind of image is it? Photo, illustration, icon, logo, product screenshot, chart, social graphic, event graphic, legal and trust imagery, anything showing a person.
3. **The content type.** Where is it going? Blog hero, LinkedIn, X, email header, landing page.

Most images touch one rule from each layer, and some touch two categories. A photo of a staff member at a customer site is photography and consent at once, and it has to pass both.

A lower layer can narrow a higher one. The illustration category accepts several formats, for example, and the blog hero page accepts fewer of them. In that case follow the narrower rule for that placement, and the broader rule stays true everywhere else. A lower layer cannot loosen this page. If a content-type page seems to let you do something this page forbids, bring it to Brand, because one of the two pages is wrong and we want to fix it.

Per-campaign exceptions go through Noor's exception log. Without an entry there, if a campaign needs something new, the rule changes for everybody or the campaign changes.

**Current identity only.** Ember `#C2501F`, Soot `#15181C`, Tallow `#F4EFE6`, with Whetstone `#5E6B73` and Verdigris `#2F8F83` as secondary colors. Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono for any type on an image. Anything leaning on the 2024 blue palette or the 2024 logo is out, however good it looks. Some of those images are still in the library with no flag on them, so your eye is part of this check.

**No third-party marks.** No real product logos on laptop lids, no cloud provider marks on diagrams, no conference logos in a crop unless the agreement with that organizer allows it. Customer marks are a legal matter and go through Legal first.

**No watermarks,** no preview overlays, no leftover crop marks. If an image arrived with a watermark, its rights are not what you think they are.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. Filters are out too: the warm look comes from the source image, and a filter laid on a cool image only makes it look cool and filtered. If an image needs a color change to fit, it is the wrong image.

**Export for the placement.** WebP or PNG for web, PNG where transparency matters, SVG for logos and icons when the placement accepts it. Keep web images under 400 KB unless the content-type page says otherwise. JPEG artifacts around Ember shapes are very visible, so check flat illustration at full size after compressing.

**Nothing that frightens.** Images follow the same stance as the copy. Show the small fire or the calm room, and skip the alarm. Red alert screens, countdown timers, sirens and skulls have no place here, even as a joke in an engineering post.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "Other rules for all images"], "ref": "s113", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "98588c52-bb4f-4b97-8b2e-da0afede6983", "content": "## 15. Usage notes

- **a/an:** go by sound. An eBPF agent, a SOC 2 report, an SRE.
- **back end** (noun), **back-end** (adjective).
- **cyber:** avoid as a prefix. Say what kind of security you mean.
- **data** is singular in our copy: "the data is".
- **drain:** a verb in Kubernetes and in our copy. "Drained the node."
- **e.g., i.e., etc.:** write "for example", "that is", or finish the list.
- **email:** no hyphen.
- **failover** (noun), **fail over** (verb).
- **in order to:** "to".
- **log in** (verb), **login** (noun). Same pattern for **set up / setup**, **roll out / rollout**, **shut down / shutdown**.
- **real time** (noun), **real-time** (adjective).
- **sidecar, service mesh:** lowercase, one and two words.
- **startup:** one word.
- **third party** (noun), **third-party** (adjective).
- **trade-off:** hyphenated.
- **utilize:** "use".
- **very, really, extremely:** delete and reread.
- **via:** "through", unless it's a technical path.
- **zero-day:** hyphenated, and only for an actual zero-day.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "15. Usage notes"], "ref": "s114", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9b333c21-ba1c-413a-bd7a-144ac492a1b9", "content": "### The brand idea

A wick is where a fire is allowed to exist. It gives the flame a place to be, and it keeps the flame there. That is the idea behind the name, the mark and the tagline. Wickhold accepts that production systems have heat in them. The job is to hold it to a small, known place.

This idea should explain design and copy decisions when a rule doesn't. When two options are both on brand, pick the one that feels calmer and more contained.

Read it out loud as a handover to the next on-call. If you stumble, or feel you are selling to a colleague, rewrite that part.

Then a few checks that catch most problems:

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "8. Typography", "The three families"], "ref": "s125", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b39ffdf9-91aa-4c47-a19d-da6e58b90e6e", "content": "## 12. Social and email formatting

- No emoji in brand posts or email. Founders can do as they like on their own accounts within reason.
- One link per post. Put it where it reads naturally; shortened links are for tracking and shouldn't appear as bare text where the full domain would fit.
- Line breaks on LinkedIn mark real paragraph breaks. No one-sentence-per-line posts.
- Greeting in email: "Hi Sam," with the first name and a comma, or no greeting for a broadcast. No "Dear". No "Hey there".
- Plain sign-off: name, job, company, or the team name on a broadcast. Nobody signs "Cheers" on a customer notice.
- In email, check that the piece reads correctly with images off.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "12. Social and email formatting"], "ref": "s126", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "b7b87728-b779-4387-aded-a12e59f856d7", "content": "## 1. Headlines

**Headlines are in sentence case.** Capitalize the first word and any proper noun. Everything else is lowercase.

This covers page titles, blog titles, section headings, email subject lines, slide titles, buttons, nav labels, form labels, table headers and any text set over an image. If it looks like a heading, it is one.

| Right | Wrong |
|---|---|
| What contain mode does to a running pod | What Contain Mode Does To A Running Pod |
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | WICKHOLD CONTAINMENT REPORT 2026 |
| How Ostler Grocers cut its open critical misconfigurations | How Ostler Grocers Cut Its Open Critical Misconfigurations |

Details:

- Product names, event names and the report title keep their capitals, as do Kubernetes, Helm, CVE and the rest of the proper vocabulary. `containerd` and `eBPF` keep their lowercase starts even as the first word, though it's nicer to rewrite so that neither opens a headline.
- The word after a colon is lowercase: "Drift: what it is and how to read it".
- No full stop on headlines. The tagline is the one exception, and it keeps its full stop everywhere.
- No code formatting in headlines. They break in email clients and in link previews.
- Keep a headline to one idea. If it needs a colon and a dash, it's two headlines.

The old sheet used Title Case for everything over 24px. That went in the rebrand, and pages still carrying it get fixed when someone next touches them.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "1. Headlines"], "ref": "s127", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ba11321a-3c46-44c9-b56c-ba0b84503c24", "content": "### Writing the company name

Write Wickhold, with one capital. The possessive is Wickhold's. The name is singular in American English, so "Wickhold is", and it never takes "the" in front of it. In a logo-free context such as a plain-text email or a form field, the name is simply typed out. Internal team names like "Wickhold Marketing" are descriptions and do not need any special treatment.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Writing the company name"], "ref": "s128", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bab04564-38bc-4e96-ba78-9bb00fa98da6", "content": "### Email and event lists

- Do not import badge scans or partner lists into a send until field marketing confirms the lawful basis for that list.
- Every EU and UK send carries an unsubscribe link and the Wickhold, Inc. postal address.
- Bought lists are not used in these regions. This was tried once in 2025 for a German webinar and dropped after the complaints.
- Event pages say who receives attendee data before the attendee registers.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy", "Email and event lists"], "ref": "s129", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bc78b090-211c-4c83-92b8-ef866c9adc03", "content": "### Say the number, then stop

Claims carry a figure and a source. No adjective stacks.

"Fast" is not a claim. "A fast, powerful, highly scalable runtime platform" is three non-claims in a row. Write the number, say where it came from, and end the sentence. The urge to add a second sentence explaining why the number is impressive is the urge to resist. A reader who needs that sentence is the wrong reader; a reader who doesn't will think less of us for it.

Bad: "Lowmoor Credit Union saw an incredible, game-changing reduction in response times."

Good: "Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes across 220 nodes."

Bad: "Quenchline is extremely lightweight and blazingly quick."

Good: "Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026."

If there is no figure, there is usually no claim, and the honest move is to describe what the product does in plain mechanical terms. "Isolates a pod's network" needs no number and no source. It's a description. "Industry-leading isolation" needs both and has neither.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "What Wickhold believes", "Say the number, then stop"], "ref": "s130", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "bd7ba1fe-13b7-4692-afd2-ef01d0dc122b", "content": "## Review

Check the last ten posts on the blog before you commit. The same image twice in a month makes the blog look thin, and readers on the index page see them side by side. Since a hero image goes out in the social card by default, check the record's `restrictions` as you would for social use.

| Product | Job | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes, using an eBPF agent | Available since September 2020 |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Cloud and cluster posture management | Available. Took this name on March 2, 2026 |

The product names came from the same idea as the company name. A quench line is the mark where hot metal is cooled and fixed. An even burn is what a well-trimmed wick gives you. The post's author proposes and the blog editor approves. The first use of a new hero in a homepage feature goes through Brand review.
", "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Who picks"], "ref": "s134", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1483026-3308-4a52-8cf9-e6314d11b35f", "content": "## 6. Grammar and punctuation

- **American spelling** in all copy, including copy going to UK and EU readers. Containerize, not containerise.
- **Oxford comma**, always. It has settled more than one argument in Kubernetes prose, where lists of nouns can double as lists of objects.
- **Active voice** with a named actor, wherever the actor is known. "Wickhold Quenchline drained the node." If the passive is hiding who did it and that person is us, it goes.
- **Tense.** Past for what happened, present for what the product does, and nothing in the future except where a date is public.
- **Contractions** are fine in the blog, on social and in email. Skip them on legal pages and in anything aimed at a board.
- **Colons** are our favorite punctuation mark and they're doing fine. Use them to introduce the fact.
- **Semicolons** at most once a page. If there are two, one wants to be a full stop.
- **Em dashes** rarely in body copy. Most are a full stop that lost its nerve. Spaced en dashes are not a substitute.
- **Parentheses** for the short aside only. If the aside matters, promote it to a sentence.
- **Quotation marks:** double, with commas and full stops inside, American style, except for literal strings in technical writing where the punctuation would change the meaning. Single quotes only inside double.
- **Italics:** titles of reports and the occasional stress only. They disappear on Soot grounds and in email.
- **Bold:** for scanning in long documents, once or twice per section. Bold on a landing page means the design isn't working.
- **Ampersands:** only in proper names. Plain "and" in headlines too.
- **"And/or"** is a legal term. Pick one.
- **Slashes** as a shortcut ("platform/security teams") get rewritten: "platform and security teams".

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "6. Grammar and punctuation"], "ref": "s135", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c1865b41-5cea-419f-8a42-5a9096193a21", "content": "### Positioning statement

For teams that run Kubernetes in production, Wickhold is the runtime security company that contains failures early. Other tools report what they saw. Wickhold products act on it, within limits the customer's team has set, and tell the team what was done.

This statement is internal. It tells writers where the company stands, and it is not customer copy. The approved public description of the company is the current boilerplate, which is kept and owned separately.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "Positioning statement"], "ref": "s136", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c28e7438-46d7-471e-b55d-ea5418751c6c", "content": "## Document posts and video

PDF document posts are off the plan, for the same reasons as carousels. Native video follows the screenshot rules for captures. A title frame counts as an image and falls under the seven-word cap.

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn images", "Document posts and video"], "ref": "s137", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/linkedin-image.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c37df191-6216-45a0-a492-50686e14a2e5", "content": "### One focal point

Every image has one focal point. A reader should be able to say what the image is of after a second's look. If two things compete, crop or pick another image.

Tests we use in review:

- Squint at it. One shape or area should hold.
- Shrink it to a thumbnail. Something should still be identifiable.
- Describe it in one short sentence without "and". "An engineer reading a terminal in a dark room" passes. "A team at a table and a wall of monitors and a logo on the door" does not.

Collages, split screens and before-and-after pairs fail this unless they are charts, where the comparison is the single point.

", "heading_path": ["Visual rules common to every image", "The two rules that come up every week", "One focal point"], "ref": "s138", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/00-visual-rules-common.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c555aa43-f86c-4b00-af8f-ab621338c84f", "content": "## 4. Certification status

SOC 2 Type II: held. Renewed January 2026. The report is shared under NDA through the account team.

FedRAMP Moderate: in process. The approved sentence is "Wickhold is pursuing FedRAMP Moderate authorization." Never state or imply FedRAMP authorization or certification. The status sheet has the detail and is the first thing to check.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "4. Certification status"], "ref": "s139", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c6394c1c-58a9-4ee0-8f7e-d115ca33d2d6", "content": "## Alt text on every image

Every image has alt text. This covers blog images, email images, landing pages, social uploads where the platform offers the field, and images in PDFs. The author of the piece writes it, because the designer usually does not know why the image is there.

Write what the reader would lose if the image failed to load. One or two plain sentences, under about 125 characters when you can manage it. Skip "image of" and "picture of". Do not stuff keywords. Do not paste the `description` field from the library: that describes the file, and alt text describes what the image is doing in this piece.

| Image | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Photo | "Engineer, Kubernetes, security, on-call, data center" | "An engineer reads a terminal in a dim equipment room." |
| Product screenshot | "Screenshot of dashboard" | "Quenchline shows one pod isolated, with network access removed and the process frozen." |
| Chart | "Bar chart" | "Median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours. Wickhold Containment Report 2026." |
| Logo | "logo.png" | "Wickhold logo" |
| Illustration | "Decorative graphic" | "A cut-paper wick with a single small Ember flame." |

Charts and screenshots carry the finding in the alt text, and the reader should not need the picture to get the number. If the chart has more than about four values, put the values in a table or the body copy under it and let the alt text state the point.

Any text set on an image must also appear in the alt text or the surrounding copy. Screen readers cannot read a stat card.

The "every image" part holds for decorative images too. If an image truly adds nothing, the first question is why it is in the piece. Background textures set in CSS are not images for this purpose and need no alt.

", "heading_path": ["Image accessibility", "Alt text on every image"], "ref": "s140", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/accessibility.md"}, {"chunk_id": "c6a52d68-5c35-45b0-aceb-b1a1e1b7e799", "content": "## 17. Accepted shortcuts and exceptions

- Internal documents (including this one) don't need to meet the citation form. They do need to be right.
- Slide speaker notes follow the same rules once they go into a shared deck, since decks get forwarded.
- Quoted customer language stays as approved, including its capitalization. If a quote has a problem, go back to the customer through the customer marketing owner; don't fix it in place.
- Text inside a screenshot is not edited. If a screenshot shows something out of date, take a new one.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "17. Accepted shortcuts and exceptions"], "ref": "s141", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca1ba113-65da-4917-9655-fa55f8b6ad6f", "content": "## Reading old copy

Pre-2026 material is everywhere: the archive, old decks, the sales team's memory. It sounds different for a reason. The old brand sold watching. It leaned on "always", "every" and "complete", and it got excited in public. A lot of it is competent copy for a company we no longer are.

If you are reusing something from before the rebrand, do not patch the sentences. Take the facts, check that they are still approved, and write it again. Look for these symptoms when reading a draft that someone has recycled: a promise of total coverage, a sentence about seeing with nothing about what happens next, and an excited tone that doesn't match the numbers beside it.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Reading old copy"], "ref": "s142", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca3468d9-9da9-4734-a3d6-9c0497716473", "content": "## 5. Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "5. Statistics: 12-month age limit"], "ref": "s143", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca490efc-da47-4269-b919-e60bd97f97e1", "content": "## Regional rules: EU and UK copy

Priit Salonen, with notes from the field marketing review, August 2026

Applies to anything aimed at readers in the EU or the UK: campaigns, event pages, email sends, localized landing pages, press outreach, partner co-marketing. If a global asset will run in those regions, it is regional copy too.

", "heading_path": ["Regional rules: EU and UK copy"], "ref": "s144", "relative_path": "brand/legal/regional-rules-eu-uk.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca8bf1aa-ced7-4c7e-871d-281a24c0f561", "content": "## 10. Links

Link text names the thing the reader will get: "the 2026 Containment Report", "the Helm values reference". The surrounding sentence should still read correctly if the link is dead. Don't link a whole sentence. Internal pages open in the same tab.

UTM parameters come from the campaign tracker, not from memory. Marketing ops reject hand-typed ones.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "10. Links"], "ref": "s145", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cb464fca-10ce-4726-92c8-69e56971c97d", "content": "## Not cleared

**Vaskell Health is not cleared.** Do not use the name, logo, people, quotes or results in anything external, and do not use them in a customer-facing deck. "A large health system" does not help, because the draft material is specific enough to identify them. The draft case study in the folder stays a draft. No approval was given, and a finished-looking layout does not change that.

Everyone else is not cleared by default. Companies seen in a contract, in a support ticket, or in a Slow Burn Summit attendee list are not references.

", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy", "Not cleared"], "ref": "s146", "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cb9cd1ab-7cf6-4dd3-84c9-391e53813754", "content": "## The character

Wickhold is someone who has been paged more often than you have and is not going to bring it up.

**Unhurried.** Nothing in our copy is urgent. A page that hurries the reader is using the same trick as the alert fatigue they came to us to get away from.

**Exact.** "Isolated the pod's network" beats "took action". "220 nodes" beats "at scale". If two engineers would argue over what a sentence means, it isn't finished.

**Unimpressed by itself.** The product is useful. Copy that gasps at it reads as though the writer has not seen it fail. We have seen it fail, and the release notes say so.

**On your side of the pager.** The reader is a peer on the same rota, and we write to them as someone who could take the next shift. No lecturing, no "did you know", no explaining Kubernetes to people who run it.

When the character slips, it usually slips into one of four people:

- **The hero.** Rushes in, saves the day, gets the credit. Early rebrand drafts leaned on firefighters and helmets until Maren pointed out that a firefighter arriving means it already went badly. The customer's on-call team is the competent party in every story we tell.
- **The prophet.** Sees doom everywhere and sells shelter from it. The whole security industry's default register, which makes it invisible to the people we want to reach.
- **The buddy.** "Hey there, Kubernetes friends." Nobody paged at 3am wants a pal.
- **The analyst.** "In today's rapidly evolving threat landscape." Sentences with no one in them. If nothing would change when the paragraph is deleted, delete it.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "The character"], "ref": "s147", "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cd94a510-5949-4cb4-ae6a-bba3ddd34472", "content": "### Raising a conflict

If two documents disagree, don't quietly pick one and move on, because the next person will hit the same thing. Follow the order of authority for the piece in hand, ship it, and then send a short note to the owner of the lower document.

A useful note says three things and takes a minute to write:

> "These two documents give different answers on the same point. I used the higher one. Can the other be updated?"

The owner corrects the lower document or explains why it stands. If the higher document is the one that's out of date, the owner of that document changes it. Nobody overrides it locally.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Raising a conflict"], "ref": "s148", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cd981fdd-c863-4776-8686-3ab4cc8e9dc8", "content": "## 8. Spoken claims, demos and records

Spoken claims count. A webinar is a publication, a sales call can end up quoted in a procurement file, and a recorded conference talk stays available for years. Speakers get the same tables as writers. Questions from the floor that go beyond them are answered with "I will get back to you", and then with an email to me.

Demo environments show synthetic data. A demo may show a containment action in contain mode, and the timing shown on screen is not a claim about customer environments. Presenters should say so if anyone asks. Screenshots from a real customer tenant are not used in any circumstance.

The owner of each asset keeps the published version, or a link to it, and the source for each figure in it for three years. When a claim is withdrawn I will send a list of the assets I know about. I do not know about all of them, so owners should search their own material.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "8. Spoken claims, demos and records"], "ref": "s149", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ced40b51-cf38-4400-ba4a-10544d338867", "content": "### Product imagery

Screenshots and diagrams show the real product and real terms. When a choice exists between a clever visual metaphor and a clear view of what the product did, show the product.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "9. Photography and illustration direction", "Product imagery"], "ref": "s150", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cefc4366-9544-4ad9-930d-06a08e27c623", "content": "### Percentages

**Percentages use digits and the % symbol.** Always, including at the start of a sentence, in headlines, in legal-reviewed copy and in speech written for a stage.

- Right: 41% of platform teams, 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations.
- Wrong: forty-one percent, 41 percent, 41 per cent, 63pc.

No space before the symbol. "Percentage points" is written out when you mean the difference between two percentages, and it's rare enough in our copy that a reviewer will ask if you're sure.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "4. Numbers", "Percentages"], "ref": "s151", "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cfd8736c-24f6-4637-a4fe-87e329a80ab5", "content": "### Wickhold Leashgate (early access)

Leashgate is in early access. Claims describe what the early access product does today. They do not describe a roadmap, and they do not give a date.

Permitted vocabulary is tool-call policy, agent identity, and the blast radius of an agent. The approved outcome statement is "limits what a compromised agent can do".

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Wickhold Leashgate (early access)"], "ref": "s152", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cff1ee61-653f-40b6-b141-8a57f205945f", "content": "### Market statistics

Name the source and the year each time. A market statistic in a headline needs its source on the same screen or page section. See section 5 for how long a statistic stays usable.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Market statistics"], "ref": "s153", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "d0c14399-2877-40a1-b9e2-08aa9c6cf979", "content": "## Anonymous examples

An unnamed customer story needs the same evidence as a named one and Legal's review of the wording. Keep the sector broad and leave out numbers that could be traced. Do not invent a composite customer.

", "heading_path": ["Customer logo and quote policy", "Anonymous examples"], "ref": "s154", "relative_path": "brand/legal/customer-logo-and-quote-policy.md"}, {"chunk_id": "d1e89004-baf1-4226-8278-0203deb6a9f7", "content": "### Why the company rebranded

The 2024 brand made a promise about watching. It suited a company that sold visibility, and it stopped fitting as the product moved on. By 2025 the feature customers talked about in renewals was the moment Wickhold Quenchline isolated a pod's network at 3am and nobody had to get out of bed. Sales calls kept going the same way: the prospect would say every tool they owned could see a problem, and then ask what happens next.

Ilse Varga-Holm, who owns the rebrand, started the work in spring 2025 with a set of about 30 customer and on-call interviews. Maren Tolliver and Dov Achterberg sat in on most of them. The clearest finding was that nobody wanted another thing watching them. They wanted the blast of an incident to be smaller and the morning after to be shorter. That finding drove every decision below.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "1. What changed in 2026", "Why the company rebranded"], "ref": "s155", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "d46b6260-77fa-4102-a897-17a53c50ada1", "content": "### Mistakes seen since launch

The single most common mistake since launch is treating Ember as the "main" color because the table calls it primary. Primary means most important, and it does not mean most area.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "7. Color", "Mistakes seen since launch"], "ref": "s156", "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "d4925866-8875-4cbd-9a6f-d1368287a31e", "content": "## Size and crop

Export at 1600x900. Most library heroes and photos are 3:2, so you will lose some height. Crop from the top and bottom, then check that the focal point has survived. A hero illustration's focal element usually sits off center and the quiet part can go. Some platforms crop preview cards further, so keep the focal point out of the outer tenth of the frame.

Do not upscale. A 1536-wide source enlarged to 1600 is about the limit, and it should look clean at full size.

", "heading_path": ["Blog hero images", "Size and crop"], "ref": "s157", "relative_path": "brand/visuals/by-content-type/blog-hero.md"}, {"chunk_id": "d5917474-5628-4710-bcee-8fc4d508b8f4", "content": "### Lab figures

Two product figures come from Wickhold's own lab. Both must carry the phrase "in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026", in the same sentence as the figure.

| Figure | Required form |
|---|---|
| CPU overhead | "under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |
| Containment speed | "contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026" |

A footnote does not meet this requirement. An asterisk does not meet it. A qualifier on the slide before does not meet it. In a chart, the phrase goes in the chart title or directly under it. In a talk, the speaker says it aloud.

The figures describe a lab, so they may not be presented as field results or customer averages. "Known-bad process" is part of the claim: it does not extend to unknown processes, novel techniques, or "threats" in general. Reports may repeat the figures only if the benchmark year stays attached. When the 2027 benchmarks run, the year changes and this table is reissued. Nobody edits the year by hand.

Approved:

> Wickhold Quenchline adds under 2% CPU overhead on a typical node in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.

Not approved:

> Quenchline contains attacks in 38 seconds.

> Under 2% overhead. Guaranteed.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Lab figures"], "ref": "s158", "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "d62a25c1-8dcf-4f5f-9fca-e5ace68eb593", "content": "### Change log
