{"brand_preferences": [], "rule_pack": {"evidence": [{"chunk_id": "06ede73b-42e2-4a1d-8774-10eb6d36ca3a", "content": "### Product behavior

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode it records what it would have done. Copy describing automatic containment must therefore be true of contain mode and should say so where a reader could assume otherwise. Containment actions are isolating a pod's network, freezing a process and draining a node. Do not add to the list without product confirmation.

Wickhold Evenburn reports drift, exposure paths and a fix order. It does not change a customer's environment by itself, and copy should not imply that it does.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Product behavior"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1539b083-de00-4738-8643-5b57c2f52acf", "content": "## Examples

Good, report post:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> That figure comes from the Wickhold Containment Report 2026, our survey of 412 platform and security leaders. The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
>
> 7.4 hours is most of an on-call shift, spent on one problem while everything else waits.
>
> Read the report: https://wickhold.example/containment-report

Good, customer post. The numbers are approved and the post leaves them alone:

> Lowmoor Credit Union runs Wickhold Quenchline across 220 nodes. Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes.
>
> Quenchline is our runtime detection and containment product for Kubernetes. It uses an eBPF agent to isolate a pod's network, freeze a process or drain a node.
>
> Read the Lowmoor story: https://wickhold.example/customers/lowmoor

Good, product post:

> Wickhold Quenchline contains a known-bad process in a median of 38 seconds in Wickhold lab benchmarks, 2026.
>
> Lab conditions are kinder than your cluster on a bad night, so start in observe mode and read what it would have done. Then pick the namespaces where contain mode earns its place.
>
> See the rollout guide: https://wickhold.example/docs/rollout

Good, posture post:

> Ostler Grocers cut open critical misconfigurations by 63% in 90 days, across 1,900 nodes.
>
> Wickhold Evenburn tracks drift across cloud and cluster, maps each exposure path, and gives the team a fix order for Monday morning.
>
> Read the Ostler story: https://wickhold.example/customers/ostler

Good openers for founder posts. Only the first lines are shown here because Maren and Dov write the rest themselves:

> The worst page I ever took was for a disk that had filled up with logs about a disk filling up.

> I spent four years on call before we started this company, and I still check my phone at 3:10am.

Bad, from a 2024 draft that came back to the queue last spring:

> We're thrilled to announce an exciting new chapter in our journey! Our amazing team has been working around the clock to bring you the future of cloud security. Stay tuned, big things are coming!

", "heading_path": ["LinkedIn playbook", "Examples"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/linkedin-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "1b2ec0a3-937b-43d7-a777-88143fa3b565", "content": "## Tone by channel

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. "Wickhold Quenchline isolates the pod, freezes the process or drains the node, then writes down what it did."

**Blog.** The most room to think. Brand-voice posts walk through how something fails. Dov's posts can argue, and they should. A good post leaves the reader able to do one thing they could not do before, even if they never buy. Avoid the summary paragraph at the end. If the post worked, the reader was there.

**LinkedIn.** The company page is brand voice. Founder posts are where the personality lives. A post runs about 200 words, which suits one story and one point. Write as a person with a job, not a thought leader: no line breaks after every sentence, no "here's what I learned", no lists of lessons from an outage.

**X.** One fact, or one observation, in a dry tone. The account does not chase the news and does not reply to arguments about vendors. It's fine for a post to be plain. "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. That is most of a night shift."

**Email.** One person writing to one person who is busy. Say why you are writing in the first sentence. Assume it is being read on a phone in a hallway. No "I hope this finds you well", and since these are brand emails, no "I" at all unless Maren signed it. Customer notices are the exception to everything else in this list and sound like the incident channel at the top of this document.

**Product UI and error text.** The closest thing we have to pure voice. What happened, what state things are in, what to do. "Containment action failed on node `ip-10-2-14-7`: agent unreachable. The pod is still running. Retry or drain the node." Chirpy empty states were tried in 2025 and came out after a customer saw one during a real incident.

**Case studies.** Third person, numbers up front, the customer's team as the subject of most sentences. Enough detail about their environment that a peer recognizes it. A case study that could describe any customer describes none of them.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "Tone by channel"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "20935a37-7df2-480f-a9e7-2b77fe6fd1fe", "content": "## 14. Bylines and bios

- Blog bylines: full name and title. "By Kofi Anselm, Head of Developer Relations".
- A byline doesn't change the voice. Posts by staff are written like every other piece of company copy. Founder posts have their own treatment, covered in the voice document.
- Bios run one sentence and state a job. Not "passionate about", not "self-described", no hobbies unless the hobby is funny enough for Noor to let it through.
- Don't feature former staff in new pieces. If someone has left, their old byline stays on their old posts.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "14. Bylines and bios"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "26f9f996-cd6d-4ef6-b3b8-972d1bd0c6c0", "content": "## 6. Review

| Step | Who | When |
|---|---|---|
| Outline | Editor (Kofi for engineering posts, Noor for the rest) | Before anyone writes 1,000 words |
| Technical read | An engineer who did not write it | Draft complete |
| Copy edit | Brand team | After the technical read |
| Claims check | Priit, for any customer, certification or number, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims | As the approved claims set out |
| Paste test | Second engineer, code posts only | Day before publish |

Allow two weeks from outline to publish. Report posts in April move faster because Legal has already checked the numbers.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "6. Review"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2c9fa907-d71a-493e-970c-0af9cbc9374b", "content": "## 9. Review, exceptions, and how this document changes

Every piece of external copy containing a claim from section 1 or 2 is reviewed against this document by its author. Copy containing a new claim, a customer name, or a reference to a security incident also comes to me. Press releases and the annual report come to me regardless.

Exceptions are given in writing, for one asset, and expire with that asset. I have given two this year. Neither should be taken as a precedent.

If this document disagrees with a guideline, a playbook, a deck or a comment from a senior colleague, this document wins. If it disagrees with reality, tell me, and I will change it.

Reviewed each quarter with Ilse Varga-Holm and Noor Eskelund.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "9. Review, exceptions, and how this document changes"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2dfe4ee1-b5b7-475f-aa8a-47e4ee921cb3", "content": "## 1. Length

Blog posts run 900 to 1,400 words. That range counts the body, including captions and code comments you wrote yourself, but not the code output you pasted.

Under 900 words, it's probably a release note or a LinkedIn post. Over 1,400 words, split it in two or cut the history section. We all write the history section first because it's easy, and nobody needs it. The report, the docs and the rollout guide are the place for anything longer.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "1. Length"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "2ed35bac-e511-4a05-b03f-f56a94ab438a", "content": "## 3. Citations

**Citations give the source name, the year and the link, in brackets, right after the claim.**

The shape, exactly:

```text
41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].
```

- Source name in full, as the source spells it.
- Comma, year. Comma, link. The full stop for the sentence goes outside the bracket.
- Link goes to the report or page itself, not a press release about it and not a search result. In a PDF or on a slide print the link out, because hyperlinks do not survive a screenshot.
- Use the same form everywhere, including LinkedIn and X. Yes, it's long on X. Plan the post around it.
- Two sources for one claim: two brackets. Do not merge them.
- A source we did not produce gets its own name in the bracket, even when a Wickhold page quotes it. Cite the original.
- In long pieces (report summaries, the blog), mention the survey base once near the first figure: "a survey of 412 platform and security leaders".

We tried numbered footnotes on the blog through most of 2025 and dropped them. The claim got quoted on LinkedIn, the footnote stayed behind, and the number went around with no source. A bracket travels with the sentence.

Customer results don't take a bracket when the customer is named in the sentence and the case study is linked from the page. Naming them is the source.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "3. Citations"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "33d10c5d-c881-4d79-95fa-1edc60d3c984", "content": "## 1. Claims approved as written

| Topic | Approved wording | Evidence held by |
|---|---|---|
| Customer count | "more than 140 customers" | Finance, reconciled quarterly |
| Market, time to contain | "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Market, median | "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" | Wickhold Containment Report 2026 |
| Lowmoor Credit Union | Time to contain fell from 4 hours to 11 minutes, 220 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| Ostler Grocers | 63% fewer open critical misconfigurations in 90 days, 1,900 nodes | Signed customer approval |
| SOC 2 | Wickhold holds SOC 2 Type II, renewed January 2026 | Legal |
| Agent policy | "limits what a compromised agent can do" | Legal and product |
| Company | Founded in March 2019 in Denver, Colorado | Legal |
| Funding | Series B of $46M in June 2024, led by Marlbank Partners | Legal |

The Containment Report was published on April 14, 2026, and surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. Give the survey size when the copy has room for it. The legal entity is Wickhold, Inc. Contracts, order forms, privacy notices and page footers use that form. Marketing copy uses Wickhold.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "1. Claims approved as written"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "3410ca50-9f2f-46c3-90e9-d1ff5cff3651", "content": "### Vocabulary that belongs to the products

Each product has a small set of terms. Use them exactly, because customers see the same words in the console.

- **Quenchline:** containment action (isolate a pod's network, freeze a process, drain a node), default containment policy, contain mode, observe mode.
- **Evenburn:** drift, exposure path, fix order.
- **Leashgate:** tool-call policy, agent identity, blast radius of an agent.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Vocabulary that belongs to the products"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "383000ed-25fc-4fa8-8a32-0a9cb7da5f80", "content": "## How the sentences go

**Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

**Verbs do the work.** Name who did what. "Quenchline froze the process" over "the process was frozen". Past tense for incidents, present tense for what the product does.

**End early.** Our most common edit is deleting the last line of a paragraph. Writers tend to add one that restates the point in a nicer rhythm. Readers don't need it. This goes double for the final line of a piece.

**Ration the fire.** The tagline is "Small fires stay small." It carries the metaphor so the copy doesn't have to. A piece gets at most one fire image, and many pieces should have none. Nothing ignites, sparks, blazes or fans the flames. Slow Burn Summit gets to keep its name.

**Plain words for plain things.** "Use", "start", "stop", "run". Reach for the fancier word and the reader assumes something is being hidden.

**Don't argue with the reader's experience.** Telling a platform engineer that alerts are overwhelming is telling them what they had for breakfast. Start from what they know and add something.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold voice and tone", "How the sentences go"], "relative_path": "brand/voice/voice-and-tone-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "43519095-47d5-42a8-b0b4-9efdf2334158", "content": "# Writing for the Wickhold blog

*Kofi Anselm wrote the first version in May 2026 for the two contractors we brought in after the Containment Report. Noor edited it in July. Send fixes to either of us.*

The blog has one job: get a platform engineer or a security lead to trust that the people here have held the pager. Traffic is a side effect. A post that gets a staff engineer to forward it to their team beats a post that ranks for a keyword and gets skimmed.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4a8bc433-313b-48fe-81f1-b9d8798bc8a8", "content": "## 7. Publishing details

- URL slug: lowercase, under 60 characters, no dates.
- Meta description: one plain sentence, under 155 characters.
- Author byline is always a real person. We retired "The Wickhold Team" as a byline in 2025 when we noticed those posts got half the reads.
- Hero images come from the design team. Send the request with your outline, not the day before.
- Tuesdays and Wednesdays. Never the same day as a release note, since they compete in the newsletter.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "7. Publishing details"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "4efa700b-1645-41eb-89bc-1d8aeb1b7fb2", "content": "### Review before publishing

Most work needs one reviewer. Riskier work needs more.

| Type of work | Review |
|---|---|
| Routine social post or email from an approved template | A peer in marketing |
| New blog post or landing page | Peer, plus Noor's team for brand |
| Any technical how-to or product detail | Developer relations |
| Anything with a new claim, statistic, customer name or certification mention | Legal, before design starts, except third-party statistics under section 5 of the approved claims |
| Anything signed by a founder | The founder personally, with no exceptions |
| Press releases | Ilse and Legal |

Legal's turnaround is set in the approved claims. Brand review takes two working days. If a deadline can't take that, say so at the start of the work and not the night before. Anything already on the approved claims list needs no further sign-off for the claim itself, which is the reason to use it word for word.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Review before publishing"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "664b063b-3dba-4a39-be64-6af03fbfbb25", "content": "### Order of authority

When two sources conflict, the higher one on this list wins:

1. **Legal-approved claims.** The approved claims, certification status, regional rules and customer quote policy owned by Priit Salonen, General Counsel.
2. **These 2026 guidelines**, together with the logo and color addendum, which has the same standing.
3. **Channel playbooks.** The working guides for each channel.
4. **Everything else.** This includes the voice and style documents, messaging, personas, product overviews, templates, sales material, meeting notes and Slack.

So the order is: legal-approved claims, then the 2026 guidelines, then channel playbooks, then everything else.

A lower source is not void. It applies wherever nothing above it speaks to the question. A template's rule, or a decision recorded in meeting notes or Slack by the person who owns the topic, is followed like any other rule until a higher source contradicts it. The order settles conflicts and does not rank importance. If a document at the bottom of the list has the only rule on a subject, that is the rule.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "11. Governance", "Order of authority"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "6fabfd1d-c817-4def-a0d5-bc9821112094", "content": "## 4. Shape of a post

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

Titles we rewrote:

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"
- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

End on the practical next step, then one call to action to the most relevant page. Don't summarize what you just said. If the post was good, they remember. Don't add a paragraph about Wickhold at the bottom either, as the footer handles that.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "4. Shape of a post"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "71def5fd-8e65-4813-946c-8576df1c15d3", "content": "## 2. First lines

**No rhetorical question as the first line of any asset.** Blog post, landing page hero, email (subject line and first sentence both), LinkedIn post, X post, video script, slide one of a deck.

"Is your cluster ready for the next incident?" tells the reader nothing and asks them to do the writer's work. It's also the most common opening in our category, so it reads as noise. Open on a fact, an event or a claim.

| Don't open with | Open with |
|---|---|
| What would you do if a pod started a shell at 3am? | A pod in `checkout` started a shell at 03:14 UTC. |
| Tired of alert fatigue? | Most alerts at 3am are about something that already stopped mattering. |

Real questions later in a piece are fine. An FAQ section is full of them and that's what it is for, as long as the page opens on a statement.

", "heading_path": ["Content style guide", "2. First lines"], "relative_path": "brand/style/content-style-guide.md"}, {"chunk_id": "7ebb4833-c358-4e50-aa82-4fa58d196656", "content": "# Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)

Pinned for the web team after three separate spellings turned up on one page.

Full form on first mention, short form after. First mention means the first place the name appears in a piece, and a headline counts.

| First mention | After that |
|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Quenchline |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Evenburn |
| Wickhold Leashgate | Leashgate |

One capital each. Never QuenchLine, EvenBurn or LeashGate. No internal caps, no hyphens, no all-caps in slides or nav.

Each piece starts over. A blog post that says Wickhold Quenchline does not earn the short form in the email promoting it.

Evenburn took its name on March 2, 2026. Don't write the former name in current copy, including "formerly" lines. Support handles customers who still ask for it.

Right: "Wickhold Evenburn ranks drift by exposure path. Evenburn does not contain anything at runtime."

Wrong: "Evenburn ranks drift" as the opening line, with the full name saved for the footer.

Nav labels and pricing table rows can use the short form. The page's first heading or sentence still uses the full one.

Never combine products into one name ("Quenchline-Evenburn suite"). There is no suite. If you mean more than one, name them.

**Company:** Wickhold. "Wickhold Security" retired with the rebrand on February 10, 2026. Wickhold, Inc. appears in contracts and legal footers and nowhere else.

**Lowercase, always:** contain mode, observe mode, containment action, default containment policy, drift, exposure path, fix order, tool-call policy, agent identity. These are concepts, not features with a logo.

**Capitalized:** tiers (Core, Team, Enterprise), Slow Burn Summit, Field Day, Wickhold Containment Report. "The report" on second reference, lowercase. Series A and Series B take capitals; SOC 2 Type II is set as shown.

Possessives are fine (Quenchline's agent). Skip the article: "Quenchline contains", never "the Quenchline".

The report had a different name before 2025: Wickhold Field Report. Keep that name when citing an edition that carried it. Don't rename old editions.

Feature names don't get "Wickhold" in front of them, and they don't get a trademark symbol. Neither do the products in running copy.

Lowercase product names only in code, where the tool demands it.
", "heading_path": ["Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)"], "relative_path": "brand/style/capitalization-product-names.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9792dec6-922e-42ef-aded-9a7b0bc70f03", "content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. The rule is there because engineers are more willing to keep reading once they know the problem is measured and someone has measured it honestly.

Statistics are subject to the age limit in the approved claims, so check the date before you reuse an intro from an older post.

Market statistics are figures about the market or a surveyed population. Our own customer results and benchmark numbers belong further down the post, and they don't satisfy this requirement.

Good:

> The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. Most of the teams we talk to can tell you how long detection took. Far fewer can tell you what happened in the hours after. This post is about those hours.

Good:

> 41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report]. A lot of that time goes to one question: who is allowed to touch the workload? Here is how to settle that question before the page goes off.

Bad, because it has no statistic and no reason to read on:

> Kubernetes has changed how modern teams ship software, and with that change come new security challenges.

Bad, because a customer result is doing the job of a market statistic:

> Lowmoor Credit Union cut time to contain from 4 hours to 11 minutes. Here's how your team can get the same results.

", "heading_path": ["Writing for the Wickhold blog", "2. The intro"], "relative_path": "brand/channels/blog-playbook.md"}, {"chunk_id": "be369cb2-7dc5-4ba7-bbea-e602c730c0e6", "content": "### Products

| Product | Job | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Quenchline | Runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes, using an eBPF agent | Available since September 2020 |
| Wickhold Evenburn | Cloud and cluster posture management | Available. Took this name on March 2, 2026 |
| Wickhold Leashgate | Runtime policy for AI agents and their tool calls | Early access since May 2026 |

The product names came from the same idea as the company name. A quench line is the mark where hot metal is cooled and fixed. An even burn is what a well-trimmed wick gives you. A leash gate is a control point an animal has to pass through on a lead. When someone asks where the names came from, those are the answers, and they make a decent line in a founder talk. They do not belong in product copy.

Spelling and capitalization of product names are covered in the style documents.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "5. Brand architecture", "Products"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "ca3468d9-9da9-4734-a3d6-9c0497716473", "content": "## 5. Statistics: 12-month age limit

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "5. Statistics: 12-month age limit"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "cff1ee61-653f-40b6-b141-8a57f205945f", "content": "### Market statistics

Name the source and the year each time. A market statistic in a headline needs its source on the same screen or page section. See section 5 for how long a statistic stays usable.

", "heading_path": ["Approved claims, 2026", "2. Claims that need a qualifier", "Market statistics"], "relative_path": "brand/legal/approved-claims-2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "eaeb3e9b-ff0b-4d03-b4dc-788697034a24", "content": "### The market problem

The strongest evidence for this position comes from Wickhold's own research. The Wickhold Containment Report 2026, published April 14, 2026, surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. It found that "41% of platform teams need more than six hours to contain a runtime incident" and that "the median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours" [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report].

The gap those numbers describe is between finding something and doing something about it. Detection has become cheap and common. Containment still depends on a person with enough access waking up, reading the alert, deciding, and acting. Wickhold's position lives in those hours.

", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The market problem"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f1e93386-bd9e-4240-9294-b61ce8701dec", "content": "## Who posts

**Company page.** Marketing runs it. Two or three posts a week, Tuesday to Thursday, usually mid-morning Mountain time. Fridays stayed on the calendar through most of 2025 and did nothing, so they came off.

**Maren and Dov.** They post from their own profiles when they have something to say. Marketing can draft, but they rewrite. Do not schedule on their behalf without a yes in writing, and do not reply to comments as them. If a draft of Maren's has been sitting for two weeks, drop it. She has decided.

**Kofi and the DevRel team.** Kofi posts from his own profile about conference talks, open-source eBPF work and whatever broke in the demo cluster. He does not need brand review for those unless a post carries a customer name, a product claim or a number.

**Everyone else.** People can share company posts however they like. We ran an employee amplification program in 2025 with a shared doc of suggested captions. Forty people posted the same sentence on the same morning and it looked exactly like that. We stopped.

The report surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. This guide looks at the work between recognizing an incident and taking a containment action.

## Detection starts a decision, not a containment action
That interval is useful to examine as a sequence rather than a single number. A team may recognize a signal, establish what it refers to, decide whether a containment action fits, and determine who can authorize it. The report’s median describes the full time to contain; it does not assign a duration to any one of those steps. For a readiness discussion, separate what the team knows from what it still needs to decide. What does the alert establish? What context would change the response? Who is responsible for choosing an action, and how will others know whether the action has been taken? Writing down those answers for a representative incident can make gaps in ownership or shared understanding easier to notice before a live response. It also keeps the measured finding in perspective: a team can use it to ask where its own response needs clarity without assuming that every incident or every delay follows the same pattern.


A detection gives a team something to investigate. Containment is a separate step: someone needs to understand what the alert describes, decide what action is appropriate, and have the authority to take it. That gap is where time can accumulate.

The figure measures time to contain, not time to detect. It does not say that every incident takes 7.4 hours, or explain the cause of each delay. It does put a number on a part of incident response teams can otherwise discuss only in general terms: the time between finding a runtime problem and containing it.

That distinction matters when you plan how a product will fit into response. Detection can tell you that something needs attention. A containment action changes the workload’s state. Teams need to know which actions are available and whether the system is set to take one or only record what it would have done.

## What Wickhold Quenchline does

Wickhold Quenchline provides runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes, using an eBPF agent. Its containment actions are specific: isolate a pod’s network, freeze a process, or drain a node.

Those actions affect different parts of a running workload. Isolating a pod’s network changes its ability to communicate. Freezing a process stops that process. Draining a node removes the node from service. The right response depends on the incident and the team’s tolerance for disruption; there is no universal action to take for every alert.

That is why “detect” and “contain” should not be used as if they mean the same thing. An alert is information to assess. A containment action is an intervention. Before relying on either automatic action or a human decision, make clear which of those states the product is in.

## Observe mode records; contain mode acts

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode, it records what it would have done. That distinction is essential: a record of a proposed action is not the same as an action taken on a live workload.

A team evaluating a response should be able to answer two plain questions: are we observing, or are we containing? And, if we are containing, which of the defined actions could apply? Keeping those questions visible helps prevent people from assuming that an alert has already changed the workload, or that an observed action has been carried out.

Observe mode gives a team a way to review what Quenchline would have done without taking that containment action. Use that time to examine the recorded responses against the team’s expectations. Would isolating the pod’s network be acceptable in that situation? Would freezing the process or draining the node create a disruption the team is not prepared to handle? These are review questions, not promises that an action will be appropriate in every case.

When the team is ready to take containment actions, contain mode is the mode that allows them. Be explicit about that change. The product behavior is different, and the difference should be clear to the people responsible for responding.

## Make the decision before the alert

A useful readiness check does not need a long playbook. Start with the actions Quenchline supports and ask the people who respond to incidents to discuss them before they are under pressure.

- For each action—isolating a pod’s network, freezing a process, or draining a node—discuss what the team would need to know before it was taken.
- Confirm that responders can tell whether Quenchline is in observe mode or contain mode.
- In observe mode, review what Quenchline records it would have done. Note where the proposed response matches the team’s expectations and where it needs discussion.
- Decide how the team will recognize a move from reviewing recorded actions to allowing containment actions.

This is not a substitute for incident-specific judgment. It is a way to surface disagreements about impact and authority while the team has time to discuss them. It also keeps a basic question from being left until the alert arrives: are we looking at a recorded proposal, or has a containment action happened?

## A practical next step

Take one recent runtime incident or a representative alert and walk through those questions with the responders. A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection

- "Everything You Need To Know About eBPF" became "What our eBPF agent can and can't see"

Section headings should still make sense if they're all someone reads. "Background" and "The solution" tell the reader nothing.

The report surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. This guide looks at the work between recognizing an incident and taking a containment action.

## Detection starts a decision, not a containment action
That interval is useful to examine as a sequence rather than a single number. A team may recognize a signal, establish what it refers to, decide whether a containment action fits, and determine who can authorize it. The report’s median describes the full time to contain; it does not assign a duration to any one of those steps. For a readiness discussion, separate what the team knows from what it still needs to decide. What does the alert establish? What context would change the response? Who is responsible for choosing an action, and how will others know whether the action has been taken? Writing down those answers for a representative incident can make gaps in ownership or shared understanding easier to notice before a live response. It also keeps the measured finding in perspective: a team can use it to ask where its own response needs clarity without assuming that every incident or every delay follows the same pattern.


A detection gives a team something to investigate. Containment is a separate step: someone needs to understand what the alert describes, decide what action is appropriate, and have the authority to take it. That gap is where time can accumulate.

The figure measures time to contain, not time to detect. It does not say that every incident takes 7.4 hours, or explain the cause of each delay. It does put a number on a part of incident response teams can otherwise discuss only in general terms: the time between finding a runtime problem and containing it.

That distinction matters when you plan how a product will fit into response. Detection can tell you that something needs attention. A containment action changes the workload’s state. Teams need to know which actions are available and whether the system is set to take one or only record what it would have done.

## What Wickhold Quenchline does

Wickhold Quenchline provides runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes, using an eBPF agent. Its containment actions are specific: isolate a pod’s network, freeze a process, or drain a node.

Those actions affect different parts of a running workload. Isolating a pod’s network changes its ability to communicate. Freezing a process stops that process. Draining a node removes the node from service. The right response depends on the incident and the team’s tolerance for disruption; there is no universal action to take for every alert.

That is why “detect” and “contain” should not be used as if they mean the same thing. An alert is information to assess. A containment action is an intervention. Before relying on either automatic action or a human decision, make clear which of those states the product is in.

## Observe mode records; contain mode acts

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode, it records what it would have done. That distinction is essential: a record of a proposed action is not the same as an action taken on a live workload.

A team evaluating a response should be able to answer two plain questions: are we observing, or are we containing? And, if we are containing, which of the defined actions could apply? Keeping those questions visible helps prevent people from assuming that an alert has already changed the workload, or that an observed action has been carried out.

Observe mode gives a team a way to review what Quenchline would have done without taking that containment action. Use that time to examine the recorded responses against the team’s expectations. Would isolating the pod’s network be acceptable in that situation? Would freezing the process or draining the node create a disruption the team is not prepared to handle? These are review questions, not promises that an action will be appropriate in every case.

When the team is ready to take containment actions, contain mode is the mode that allows them. Be explicit about that change. The product behavior is different, and the difference should be clear to the people responsible for responding.

## Make the decision before the alert

A useful readiness check does not need a long playbook. Start with the actions Quenchline supports and ask the people who respond to incidents to discuss them before they are under pressure.

- For each action—isolating a pod’s network, freezing a process, or draining a node—discuss what the team would need to know before it was taken.
- Confirm that responders can tell whether Quenchline is in observe mode or contain mode.
- In observe mode, review what Quenchline records it would have done. Note where the proposed response matches the team’s expectations and where it needs discussion.
- Decide how the team will recognize a move from reviewing recorded actions to allowing containment actions.

This is not a substitute for incident-specific judgment. It is a way to surface disagreements about impact and authority while the team has time to discuss them. It also keeps a basic question from being left until the alert arrives: are we looking at a recorded proposal, or has a containment action happened?

## A practical next step

Take one recent runtime incident or a representative alert and walk through those questions with the responders. Identify which of the three actions would need the most discussion, and what information the team would want before allowing it. Then review the rollout steps with the people who will operate Quenchline.

The voice stays the same. How much of it you get changes with the room.

**Landing pages.** The flattest we get. Mechanical, confident, short. The reader is deciding whether to spend ten more minutes, so tell them what the thing does on a cluster and let them go. **Short first.** Most sentences run under twenty words. The long ones earn it by carrying a real sequence of events.

When two sources conflict, the higher one on this list wins:

1. **Legal-approved claims.** The approved claims, certification status, regional rules and customer quote policy owned by Priit Salonen, General Counsel.

A title that says what the reader will get. Then the intro. Then three to five sections with descriptive headings. Then an ending that tells the reader what to do on Monday.

Titles we liked:

- Contain mode, one namespace at a time
- What drift looks like after a Helm upgrade
- The six hours after detection
- Writing your first tool-call policy for Wickhold Leashgate, in early access

- "5 Kubernetes Security Mistakes You're Making Right Now" became "Five findings we see in most new clusters"

**No rhetorical question as the first line of any asset.** Blog post, landing page hero, email (subject line and first sentence both), LinkedIn post, X post, video script, slide one of a deck.

"Is your cluster ready for the next incident?" tells the reader nothing and asks them to do the writer's work. It's also the most common opening in our category, so it reads as noise. Open on a fact, an event or a claim.

|---|---|

| Wickhold Evenburn | Evenburn |
| Wickhold Leashgate | Leashgate |

", "heading_path": ["Capitalization + product names (quick sheet)"], "relative_path": "brand/style/capitalization-product-names.md"}, {"chunk_id": "9792dec6-922e-42ef-aded-9a7b0bc70f03", "content": "## 2. The intro

A blog intro must cite a market statistic. Put it in the first two sentences, in the citation format from the style guide, and follow it with one sentence that says why this post exists. |---|---|---|

A market statistic may not be older than 12 months at publication. This is the limit on how old a statistic can be, and it is measured on the day the piece goes out, not the day it was drafted. A post queued in March for release in May is checked against May.

The limit applies to market and survey statistics only. It covers any figure that describes the industry, the market, or a population of teams. It does not apply to customer results such as the Lowmoor and Ostler outcomes, or to product metrics such as the lab figures, which have their own qualifier.

The age of a statistic runs from the publication date of its source. Fieldwork dates do not matter. A report re-quoted in a newer article keeps its original date, so a 2026 article quoting a 2024 survey is a 2024 statistic.

Applied to our own reports:

| Source | Published | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Wickhold Containment Report 2026 | April 14, 2026 | Usable for publication through April 14, 2027 |
| Wickhold Field Report 2024 | 2024 | Past the 12 months limit |
| Wickhold Field Report 2023 | 2023 | Past the 12 months limit |

The two Containment Report statistics in section 1 are the only market statistics of ours inside the limit today. The Field Report figures still appear in old decks and old posts. That is an archive problem and not a permission. Do not reuse them. Do not reword them to make them feel new, and do not refer to them as "historically" true.

Fresh third-party statistics are allowed without coming to me first, with the source link and the date of the source in the copy. The source must be a named publisher and the figure must appear on the page you link to. A figure found in a vendor's blog, quoting another vendor's blog, gets traced to the original or is dropped. The third party's name still has to clear the competitor rules.

When the 2027 Containment Report is published, section 1 will be updated and the 2026 figures remain usable until they reach the limit. Old assets stay in the archive as they are. They are not re-promoted once a market statistic in them has expired. Paid and email reuse counts as publication.

The strongest evidence for this position comes from Wickhold's own research. The Wickhold Containment Report 2026, published April 14, 2026, surveyed 412 platform and security leaders. ", "heading_path": ["Wickhold brand guidelines 2026", "4. Positioning", "The market problem"], "relative_path": "brand/guidelines/Brand_Guidelines_2026.md"}, {"chunk_id": "f1e93386-bd9e-4240-9294-b61ce8701dec", "content": "## Who posts

**Kofi and the DevRel team.** Kofi posts from his own profile about conference talks, open-source eBPF work and whatever broke in the demo cluster. He does not need brand review for those unless a post carries a customer name, a product claim or a number.

**Everyone else.** People can share company posts however they like. We ran an employee amplification program in 2025 with a shared doc of suggested captions. Forty people posted the same sentence on the same morning and it looked exactly like that. We stopped.

Review the content angles below, adjust them in chat, or choose Approve & generate."}], "current_decisions": [], "draft": {"body": "The median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours [Wickhold Containment Report, 2026, https://wickhold.example/containment-report] (based on a survey of 412 platform and security leaders). This guide looks at the work between recognizing an incident and taking a containment action.

## Detection starts a decision, not a containment action
That interval is useful to examine as a sequence rather than a single number. A team may recognize a signal, establish what it refers to, decide whether a containment action fits, and determine who can authorize it. The report’s median describes the full time to contain; it does not assign a duration to any one of those steps. For a readiness discussion, separate what the team knows from what it still needs to decide. What does the alert establish? What context would change the response? Who is responsible for choosing an action, and how will others know whether the action has been taken? Writing down those answers for a representative incident can make gaps in ownership or shared understanding easier to notice before a live response. It also keeps the measured finding in perspective: a team can use it to ask where its own response needs clarity without assuming that every incident or every delay follows the same pattern.


A detection gives a team something to investigate. Containment is a separate step: someone needs to understand what the alert describes, decide what action is appropriate, and have the authority to take it. That gap is where time can accumulate.

The figure measures time to contain, not time to detect. It does not say that every incident takes 7.4 hours, or explain the cause of each delay. It does put a number on a part of incident response teams can otherwise discuss only in general terms: the time between finding a runtime problem and containing it.

That distinction matters when you plan how a product will fit into response. Detection can tell you that something needs attention. A containment action changes the workload’s state. Teams need to know which actions are available and whether the system is set to take one or only record what it would have done.

## What Wickhold Quenchline does

Wickhold Quenchline provides runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes, using an eBPF agent. Its containment actions are specific: isolate a pod’s network, freeze a process, or drain a node.

Those actions affect different parts of a running workload. Isolating a pod’s network changes its ability to communicate. Freezing a process stops that process. Draining a node removes the node from service. The right response depends on the incident and the team’s tolerance for disruption; there is no universal action to take for every alert.

That is why “detect” and “contain” should not be used as if they mean the same thing. An alert is information to assess. A containment action is an intervention. Before relying on either automatic action or a human decision, make clear which of those states the product is in.

## Observe mode records; contain mode acts

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode, it records what it would have done. That distinction is essential: a record of a proposed action is not the same as an action taken on a live workload.

A team evaluating a response should be able to answer two plain questions: are we observing, or are we containing? And, if we are containing, which of the defined actions could apply? Keeping those questions visible helps prevent people from assuming that an alert has already changed the workload, or that an observed action has been carried out.

Observe mode gives a team a way to review what Quenchline would have done without taking that containment action. Use that time to examine the recorded responses against the team’s expectations. Would isolating the pod’s network be acceptable in that situation? Would freezing the process or draining the node create a disruption the team is not prepared to handle? These are review questions, not promises that an action will be appropriate in every case.

When the team is ready to take containment actions, contain mode is the mode that allows them. Be explicit about that change. The product behavior is different, and the difference should be clear to the people responsible for responding.

## Make the decision before the alert

A useful readiness check does not need a long playbook. Start with the actions Quenchline supports and ask the people who respond to incidents to discuss them before they are under pressure.

- For each action—isolating a pod’s network, freezing a process, or draining a node—discuss what the team would need to know before it was taken.
- Confirm that responders can tell whether Quenchline is in observe mode or contain mode.
- In observe mode, review what Quenchline records it would have done. Note where the proposed response matches the team’s expectations and where it needs discussion.
- Decide how the team will recognize a move from reviewing recorded actions to allowing containment actions.

This is not a substitute for incident-specific judgment. It is a way to surface disagreements about impact and authority while the team has time to discuss them. It also keeps a basic question from being left until the alert arrives: are we looking at a recorded proposal, or has a containment action happened?

## A practical next step

Take one recent runtime incident or a representative alert and walk through those questions with the responders. Identify which of the three actions would need the most discussion, and what information the team would want before allowing it. Then review the rollout steps with the people who will operate Quenchline.

This guide looks at the work between recognizing an incident and taking a containment action.

## Detection starts a decision, not a containment action
That interval is useful to examine as a sequence rather than a single number. A team may recognize a signal, establish what it refers to, decide whether a containment action fits, and determine who can authorize it. The report’s median describes the full time to contain; it does not assign a duration to any one of those steps. For a readiness discussion, separate what the team knows from what it still needs to decide. What does the alert establish? What context would change the response? Who is responsible for choosing an action, and how will others know whether the action has been taken? Writing down those answers for a representative incident can make gaps in ownership or shared understanding easier to notice before a live response. It also keeps the measured finding in perspective: a team can use it to ask where its own response needs clarity without assuming that every incident or every delay follows the same pattern.


A detection gives a team something to investigate. Containment is a separate step: someone needs to understand what the alert describes, decide what action is appropriate, and have the authority to take it. That gap is where time can accumulate.

The figure measures time to contain, not time to detect. It does not say that every incident takes 7.4 hours, or explain the cause of each delay. It does put a number on a part of incident response teams can otherwise discuss only in general terms: the time between finding a runtime problem and containing it.

That distinction matters when you plan how a product will fit into response. Detection can tell you that something needs attention. A containment action changes the workload’s state. Teams need to know which actions are available and whether the system is set to take one or only record what it would have done.

## What Wickhold Quenchline does

Wickhold Quenchline provides runtime detection and containment for Kubernetes, using an eBPF agent. Its containment actions are specific: isolate a pod’s network, freeze a process, or drain a node.

Those actions affect different parts of a running workload. Isolating a pod’s network changes its ability to communicate. Freezing a process stops that process. Draining a node removes the node from service. The right response depends on the incident and the team’s tolerance for disruption; there is no universal action to take for every alert.

That is why “detect” and “contain” should not be used as if they mean the same thing. An alert is information to assess. A containment action is an intervention. Before relying on either automatic action or a human decision, make clear which of those states the product is in.

## Observe mode records; contain mode acts

Wickhold Quenchline takes a containment action only in contain mode. In observe mode, it records what it would have done. That distinction is essential: a record of a proposed action is not the same as an action taken on a live workload.

A team evaluating a response should be able to answer two plain questions: are we observing, or are we containing? And, if we are containing, which of the defined actions could apply? Keeping those questions visible helps prevent people from assuming that an alert has already changed the workload, or that an observed action has been carried out.

Observe mode gives a team a way to review what Quenchline would have done without taking that containment action. Use that time to examine the recorded responses against the team’s expectations. Would isolating the pod’s network be acceptable in that situation? Would freezing the process or draining the node create a disruption the team is not prepared to handle? These are review questions, not promises that an action will be appropriate in every case.

When the team is ready to take containment actions, contain mode is the mode that allows them. Be explicit about that change. The product behavior is different, and the difference should be clear to the people responsible for responding.

A useful readiness check does not need a long playbook. Start with the actions Quenchline supports and ask the people who respond to incidents to discuss them before they are under pressure.

- For each action—isolating a pod’s network, freezing a process, or draining a node—discuss what the team would need to know before it was taken.

{"visual_rules": {"bc413726fa21d9dc": "# Visual rules common to every image

Owner: Noor Eskelund, Head of Brand. Last edited September 2026, after the Slow Burn Summit push showed us how many people pick images without opening the metadata.

These rules apply to every image Wickhold publishes: a blog hero, a chart in a white paper, a slide a sales engineer drops into a customer call, a banner at a Field Day. If you are holding an image and wondering whether this page applies, it does.


## The spec

- **1200x627.** Export at exactly this size. Anything else gets cropped by the platform, and the crop rarely helps
- **At most seven words of overlay text**
- **Overlay text is added in design**, as live type in the template, over a finished image

Seven words means seven, counted the plain way. A hyphenated word is one word, and a number is one word. The logo does not count. A source line does count, so most stat images move the source into the post copy, which is where we want it anyway.

The seven-word cap narrows what the social graphics rules allow. A stat card on any other surface can carry a measure line and a source. On LinkedIn it gets the number and the short label only.

| Overlay | Words | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Small fires stay small. | 4 | Good |
| Median time to contain: 7.4 hours | 6 | Good, source in the post |
| 11 minutes, down from 4 hours | 6 | Good, with Lowmoor named in the post |
| Contain first. Then find out what happened. | 7 | Good |
| What Wickhold learned from surveying 412 platform and security leaders | 10 | Too long |
| Is your team ready for a runtime incident? | 8 | Too long, and it is a question |


## Checks

- 1200x627 exactly
- Count the words
- Overlay legible at phone width
- Image record read, including `restrictions`

The picture should still make sense with the post text collapsed, since the image is often all a reader sees before "see more".

The most common error in the last quarter was a logo dropped on without checking the ground. The second was a stat shortened until it no longer said what the source said. If shortening changes the meaning, use a different stat or use no overlay.

## Picking an image: the order

1. Decide the category and read that page.
2. Decide the content type and read that page.
3. Search the library. Search by description and by a few different words, since tags are uneven.
4. Open the record. Read `restrictions` and `usage_rights` first, then `background`, `safe_on` and size.
5. Look at the picture itself at full size against the current identity. Metadata does not catch everything.
6. Check it against the rest of the layout, on the real ground.
7. Add it to the draft with its `id` noted in the review comment, so Brand can trace it.


## The image library and its metadata

Every approved image lives in the image library, and every image in it has a metadata record. Do not pick from the thumbnail grid and stop there. The thumbnail does not show you the limits on the image.

| Field | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| `id`, `filename` | Identity. Filenames were set by different people across several years and tell you little. |
| `type`, `title` | Rough category and a human label. |
| `description` | What is in the picture. Often thin, sometimes empty. |
| `tags` | Search help. Inconsistent, so never treat a missing tag as meaning anything. |
| `usage_rights` | The grant we hold for the file. |
| `restrictions` | The limits on this particular image. See below. |
| `added_date` | When it entered the library, which is not when it was made. |
| `source`, `attribution` | Where it came from. In-house work reads `internal-production`, and `attribution` is usually empty or names the in-house team. Empty attribution means no credit line is needed. |
| `width`, `height` | Pixel size. Check before you plan a crop. |
| `background` | How the image relates to what sits behind it. See below. |
| `safe_on` | Which grounds it can sit on. See below. |
| `variant_of` | Points at the parent when the image is one version of another. |


## Other rules for all images

**Current identity only.** Ember `#C2501F`, Soot `#15181C`, Tallow `#F4EFE6`, with Whetstone `#5E6B73` and Verdigris `#2F8F83` as secondary colors. Bricolage Grotesque, IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono for any type on an image. Anything leaning on the 2024 blue palette or the 2024 logo is out, however good it looks. Some of those images are still in the library with no flag on them, so your eye is part of this check.

**No third-party marks.** No real product logos on laptop lids, no cloud provider marks on diagrams, no conference logos in a crop unless the agreement with that organizer allows it. Customer marks are a legal matter and go through Legal first.

**No watermarks,** no preview overlays, no leftover crop marks. If an image arrived with a watermark, its rights are not what you think they are.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. Filters are out too: the warm look comes from the source image, and a filter laid on a cool image only makes it look cool and filtered. If an image needs a color change to fit, it is the wrong image.

**Export for the placement.** WebP or PNG for web, PNG where transparency matters, SVG for logos and icons when the placement accepts it. Keep web images under 400 KB unless the content-type page says otherwise. JPEG artifacts around Ember shapes are very visible, so check flat illustration at full size after compressing.

**Nothing that frightens.** Images follow the same stance as the copy. Show the small fire or the calm room, and skip the alarm. Red alert screens, countdown timers, sirens and skulls have no place here, even as a joke in an engineering post.


## Checks before publishing

- Alt text present and written for this placement
- Text on image measured, with the worst spot checked
- Image still makes sense at 320px wide
- Meaning does not depend on color alone

### One focal point

Every image has one focal point. A reader should be able to say what the image is of after a second's look. If two things compete, crop or pick another image.

Tests we use in review:

- Squint at it. One shape or area should hold.
- Shrink it to a thumbnail. Something should still be identifiable.
- Describe it in one short sentence without "and". "An engineer reading a terminal in a dark room" passes. "A team at a table and a wall of monitors and a logo on the door" does not.

Collages, split screens and before-and-after pairs fail this unless they are charts, where the comparison is the single point.


## Alt text on every image

Every image has alt text. This covers blog images, email images, landing pages, social uploads where the platform offers the field, and images in PDFs. The author of the piece writes it, because the designer usually does not know why the image is there.

Write what the reader would lose if the image failed to load. One or two plain sentences, under about 125 characters when you can manage it. Skip "image of" and "picture of". Do not stuff keywords. Do not paste the `description` field from the library: that describes the file, and alt text describes what the image is doing in this piece.

| Image | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Photo | "Engineer, Kubernetes, security, on-call, data center" | "An engineer reads a terminal in a dim equipment room." |
| Product screenshot | "Screenshot of dashboard" | "Quenchline shows one pod isolated, with network access removed and the process frozen." |
| Chart | "Bar chart" | "Median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours. Wickhold Containment Report 2026." |
| Logo | "logo.png" | "Wickhold logo" |
| Illustration | "Decorative graphic" | "A cut-paper wick with a single small Ember flame." |

Charts and screenshots carry the finding in the alt text, and the reader should not need the picture to get the number. If the chart has more than about four values, put the values in a table or the body copy under it and let the alt text state the point.

Any text set on an image must also appear in the alt text or the surrounding copy. Screen readers cannot read a stat card.

The "every image" part holds for decorative images too. If an image truly adds nothing, the first question is why it is in the piece. Background textures set in CSS are not images for this purpose and need no alt.


## Format

- A LinkedIn post is 180 words at most. Count everything, including the link line.
- About the first 200 characters show before the "see more" cut on most phones. The news has to fit in that space.
- Short paragraphs, one to three lines each, with a blank line between them.
- One link per post, at the end, on its own line. We tested putting links in the first comment for six weeks in 2025 and could not see a difference, and it annoyed people, so links stay in the post.
- Tag a customer only after their marketing contact has seen the post. Tag people, not company pages, when a named person spoke or wrote the thing.
- Use bullets only for real lists: three containment actions, the tiers, the steps of a rollout. A post that is all bullets reads as a slide.
- Image guidance sits with the visual rules. Every company page post gets one image, except short hiring notes.


### `restrictions`: check it before every use

Read `restrictions` before you use an image, every time, including images you have used before. Restrictions are added after an image enters the library, so last quarter's check does not count.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **Retirement.** The image is deprecated and must not be used. Some retired files look entirely normal in the grid and carry no other sign. Their tags and titles may even look current.
- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

An empty `restrictions` field means nobody has recorded a limit. It does not mean the image is on brand. The field is one check among several, and the current-identity rule above still has to pass on your own judgment.

If `restrictions` and `tags` seem to disagree, `restrictions` wins. If `restrictions` and `description` disagree, stop and ask.


## What goes in the frame

Use, in rough order of how well they have done for us:

1. A photo of real work, with no overlay at all
2. A stat card from the social templates. Quote cards rarely fit the cap
3. A short product crop showing one action, large enough to read in the feed
4. A hero illustration, cropped

Library images are 3:2, so a 1200x627 crop loses about a fifth of the height. Keep the focal point near the vertical center. Spot illustrations should sit on a solid Tallow or Soot layout from the template. They are transparent and LinkedIn will show them on its own background if you upload them as they are.

Do not run overlay text across a photo's focal point. Text goes on a solid band or in the quiet side of the frame.


## By account

**Company page.** Follows all of the above. Logo present on designed images, absent on plain photos.

**Founder accounts.** Maren's and Dov's posts take a plain photo or no image. Designed cards with a company logo look like an ad under a personal post, so skip them. No overlay text on founder images unless Maren asks for it.

**Staff.** Anyone can use the approved templates. Reshare the file as it is.

- **No abstract backgrounds.** They have no focal point on their own, and a hero has no type set over it.

**No watermarks,** no preview overlays, no leftover crop marks. If an image arrived with a watermark, its rights are not what you think they are.

**Do not stretch, tint or recolor library files.** Crop freely within the category's limits. Stretching breaks the proportions of the art and recoloring breaks the palette. Filters are out too: the warm look comes from the source image, and a filter laid on a cool image only makes it look cool and filtered. If an image needs a color change to fit, it is the wrong image.

**Export for the placement.** WebP or PNG for web, PNG where transparency matters, SVG for logos and icons when the placement accepts it. Keep web images under 400 KB unless the content-type page says otherwise. JPEG artifacts around Ember shapes are very visible, so check flat illustration at full size after compressing.

**Nothing that frightens.** Images follow the same stance as the copy. Show the small fire or the calm room, and skip the alarm. Red alert screens, countdown timers, sirens and skulls have no place here, even as a joke in an engineering post.


# Blog hero images

Content team working rules, June 2026.

**Every blog post has one hero. It is a 16:9 illustration or photo. It is never a dashboard.**

Product UI in the hero looks like an ad on top of an article, and the detail goes illegible at the size most people see it, which is the preview card. If a post is about a product screen, put the screenshot in the body, at a size where it can be read.


## Checks before publishing

- Alt text present and written for this placement
- Text on image measured, with the worst spot checked
- Image still makes sense at 320px wide
- Meaning does not depend on color alone

## Avoiding repeats

Check the last ten posts on the blog before you commit. The same image twice in a month makes the blog look thin, and readers on the index page see them side by side. Since a hero image goes out in the social card by default, check the record's `restrictions` as you would for social use.


### One focal point

Every image has one focal point. A reader should be able to say what the image is of after a second's look. If two things compete, crop or pick another image.

Tests we use in review:

- Squint at it. One shape or area should hold.
- Shrink it to a thumbnail. Something should still be identifiable.
- Describe it in one short sentence without "and". "An engineer reading a terminal in a dark room" passes. "A team at a table and a wall of monitors and a logo on the door" does not.

Collages, split screens and before-and-after pairs fail this unless they are charts, where the comparison is the single point.


## Alt text on every image

Every image has alt text. This covers blog images, email images, landing pages, social uploads where the platform offers the field, and images in PDFs. The author of the piece writes it, because the designer usually does not know why the image is there.

Write what the reader would lose if the image failed to load. One or two plain sentences, under about 125 characters when you can manage it. Skip "image of" and "picture of". Do not stuff keywords. Do not paste the `description` field from the library: that describes the file, and alt text describes what the image is doing in this piece.

| Image | Bad | Good |
|---|---|---|
| Photo | "Engineer, Kubernetes, security, on-call, data center" | "An engineer reads a terminal in a dim equipment room." |
| Product screenshot | "Screenshot of dashboard" | "Quenchline shows one pod isolated, with network access removed and the process frozen." |
| Chart | "Bar chart" | "Median time to contain a runtime incident is 7.4 hours. Wickhold Containment Report 2026." |
| Logo | "logo.png" | "Wickhold logo" |
| Illustration | "Decorative graphic" | "A cut-paper wick with a single small Ember flame." |

Charts and screenshots carry the finding in the alt text, and the reader should not need the picture to get the number. If the chart has more than about four values, put the values in a table or the body copy under it and let the alt text state the point.

Any text set on an image must also appear in the alt text or the surrounding copy. Screen readers cannot read a stat card.

The "every image" part holds for decorative images too. If an image truly adds nothing, the first question is why it is in the piece. Background textures set in CSS are not images for this purpose and need no alt.


## Size and crop

Export at 1600x900. Most library heroes and photos are 3:2, so you will lose some height. Crop from the top and bottom, then check that the focal point has survived. A hero illustration's focal element usually sits off center and the quiet part can go. Some platforms crop preview cards further, so keep the focal point out of the outer tenth of the frame.

Do not upscale. A 1536-wide source enlarged to 1600 is about the limit, and it should look clean at full size.


### `restrictions`: check it before every use

Read `restrictions` before you use an image, every time, including images you have used before. Restrictions are added after an image enters the library, so last quarter's check does not count.

The field is free text, written by whoever had the reason. There is no fixed vocabulary, so read the sentence instead of searching for a keyword. Three kinds of note turn up in practice:

- **Retirement.** The image is deprecated and must not be used. Some retired files look entirely normal in the grid and carry no other sign. Their tags and titles may even look current.
- **A limited context.** The image may be used in the named context and nowhere else. A note limiting an image to internal use keeps it out of anything a customer, a prospect or the press will see, and that includes sales decks.
- **A person or place.** Something about who or what is shown has changed.

A restriction binds even when the image would be perfect, when a senior person asks for it, and when you found it already published somewhere. If you think one is out of date, ask Brand to change the record. Do not use the image and sort it out later.

An empty `restrictions` field means nobody has recorded a limit. It does not mean the image is on brand. The field is one check among several, and the current-identity rule above still has to pass on your own judgment.

If `restrictions` and `tags` seem to disagree, `restrictions` wins. If `restrictions` and `description` disagree, stop and ask.
